q: Using the graph, what is the approximate normal boiling point of Liquid 2?
e: The normal boiling point is where vapor pressure equals 760 mmHg (1 atm).

q: Looking down the C–C bond of ethane, why is the eclipsed conformation higher in energy than the staggered one?
o: Torsional strain from aligned C–H bonds
Angle strain from bonds squeezed below 109.5°
Steric clash between bulky methyl groups
Loss of π overlap between the two carbons
e: In the eclipsed form, the C–H bonds on the front and back carbons line up, and their electron pairs repel.
This is torsional strain (about 12 kJ mol⁻¹ for ethane). Ethane has no methyl groups to clash, and no π bond.

q: Isomers that have the same atom connectivity but differ in the 3-D arrangement of their atoms are called:
e: Constitutional isomers differ in which atoms are bonded to which.
Stereoisomers keep the same connectivity and differ only in spatial arrangement (enantiomers, diastereomers, cis/trans isomers).

q: Looking down the C2–C3 bond of butane, which conformation is highest in energy?
o: Eclipsed, with the two methyls aligned (0°)
Eclipsed, with each methyl aligned with an H
e: All eclipsed forms have torsional strain; lining up the two CH₃ groups adds the most steric strain as well.
Energy order: anti (lowest) < gauche < CH₃/H eclipsed < CH₃/CH₃ eclipsed (highest).

q: The pure (R) enantiomer has [α] = +40°. A sample shows +20°. What is its enantiomeric excess?
e: ee = observed ÷ pure × 100 = 20 ÷ 40 × 100 = 50%.

q: An enantiomer has a specific rotation of +25°. What is the specific rotation of its mirror image?
e: Enantiomers rotate light by equal amounts in opposite directions.

q: When assigning R/S, what should you do if the lowest-priority group points toward you?
o: Determine the direction, then reverse it
e: The rule assumes the lowest priority points away. If it points toward you, flip your answer.

q: A mixture is 75% (R) and 25% (S) of a compound. What is its enantiomeric excess?
e: ee = % major − % minor = 75 − 25 = 50%.

q: A molecule has 3 chiral centers and no internal plane of symmetry. What is the maximum number of stereoisomers?
e: Maximum stereoisomers = 2ⁿ, where n = number of chiral centers.
Meso compounds (with an internal mirror plane) would lower this count, but the question rules them out.
t: 2ⁿ is a maximum. If the molecule can have a mirror plane, expect fewer.

q: Which carbon in 2-chlorobutane, CH₃CHClCH₂CH₃, is a chiral center?
o: None; it has no chiral center
e: C2 is bonded to H, Cl, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃: four different groups.
C1 has three H's and C3 has two H's, so neither is chiral.

q: Rank these groups from highest to lowest CIP priority: –CH₂OH, –CHO, –OH, –CH₃.
e: First atoms: O beats C, so –OH is highest.
Among the carbons, compare attached atoms: –CHO has (O, O, H) because the C=O counts O twice; –CH₂OH has (O, H, H); –CH₃ has (H, H, H).
So –OH > –CHO > –CH₂OH > –CH₃.
t: A double bond to O counts as two O's in CIP rules.

q: For cis-1-tert-butyl-4-methylcyclohexane, which arrangement does the favored chair have?
e: In a cis-1,4-disubstituted cyclohexane, either chair has one group axial and one equatorial.
An axial tert-butyl costs about 20 kJ mol⁻¹ of 1,3-diaxial strain, versus about 7 kJ mol⁻¹ for methyl, so tert-butyl takes the equatorial position and the methyl is forced axial.
t: tert-Butyl acts as a conformational 'anchor': it is essentially always equatorial.

q: Diastereomers are stereoisomers that:
o: Are not mirror images of each other
e: For compounds with several stereocenters, diastereomers differ at some, but not all, of them.
Cis/trans (E/Z) alkene isomers are also diastereomers.

q: A mixture of benzoic acid, aniline and naphthalene in ether is washed with dilute HCl and then dilute NaOH. Which compound stays in the ether layer?
e: It's neutral, so neither acid nor base washes affect it.

q: A developed TLC plate is viewed under a 254 nm UV lamp, and dark spots appear. Which compounds are most easily seen this way?
e: The plate contains a fluorescent indicator that glows green under 254 nm light.
Compounds that absorb UV (aromatic rings, conjugated π systems) block the glow and look dark. Saturated compounds need a stain such as iodine or KMnO₄.

q: In liquid–liquid extraction, two layers form because the solvents:
e: Example: water and diethyl ether.

q: A solid dissolves well in hot ethanol but also fairly well in cold ethanol, and it is insoluble in water. How can a mixed-solvent recrystallization be done?
o: Dissolve in minimal hot ethanol, add hot water until cloudy, then cool
Dissolve in cold water, add hot ethanol until clear, then heat
Dissolve in hot water, add ice-cold ethanol, then filter right away
Dissolve in hot ethanol, then evaporate all of the ethanol away
e: Ethanol is the 'good' solvent and water (miscible with ethanol) is the 'poor' solvent.
Adding water until the hot solution turns cloudy makes it just saturated; slow cooling then gives crystals. Evaporating to dryness keeps the impurities too.

q: An ideal liquid mixture is 50 mol% A (pure vapor pressure 600 torr) and 50 mol% B (pure vapor pressure 200 torr). Its vapor is condensed, and the condensate is vaporized again, as on two ideal plates of a fractional column. What is the mole fraction of A in the second vapor?
e: Second vapor from a 0.75 : 0.25 liquid: P(A) = 450, P(B) = 50 → x(A) = 450 ÷ 500 = 0.90. Each cycle enriches the more volatile component.

q: A carboxylic acid streaks badly on silica TLC. Adding about 1% acetic acid to the eluent gives a tight spot. Why?
o: It keeps the compound fully protonated, so it moves as one form
It converts the compound into a less polar ester on the plate
It deprotonates the compound so it binds the silica less
It makes the silica nonpolar, so every compound moves faster
e: Without added acid, some molecules are neutral (RCOOH) and some are ionized (RCOO⁻); the two forms have very different R<sub>f</sub> values, so the spot smears.
Excess acetic acid suppresses ionization (Le Châtelier), so the compound runs as neutral RCOOH in one compact spot.

q: Recrystallization purifies a solid by:
o: Dissolving it in hot solvent and letting pure crystals form on cooling
Dissolving it in cold solvent and letting pure crystals form on heating
Melting it and collecting the pure liquid that distills over
Dissolving it in solvent and then evaporating it quickly to dryness
e: Impurities stay dissolved in the cold solvent.

q: An organic amine in an ether layer is shaken with aqueous HCl. Where does the amine go?
o: Into the aqueous layer, as an ammonium salt
It forms a solid at the interface
e: Protonation makes it charged and water-soluble.

q: On a silica TLC plate developed in hexane, all the spots stay near the baseline. Which change should move them farther up the plate?
o: Add ethyl acetate to make the eluent more polar
Use pure pentane to make the eluent less polar
Use a longer plate with the same hexane
Spot a larger amount of the sample
e: A more polar mobile phase competes better with the silica for the compounds, so they spend more time moving.
All R<sub>f</sub> values rise. A longer plate does not change R<sub>f</sub>.

q: A compound's solubility is 5.0 g per 100 mL of a solvent at its boiling point and 0.50 g per 100 mL at 0 °C. A student dissolves 5.0 g in 100 mL of the hot solvent and cools it to 0 °C. What is the maximum mass of crystals that can be recovered?
e: At 0 °C, 0.50 g stays dissolved in the 100 mL and is lost in the filtrate.
Maximum recovery = 5.0 − 0.50 = 4.5 g (90%).

q: A mixture of pentane, hexane and heptane is analyzed by GC on a nonpolar column. In which order do they elute?
o: All three at the same retention time
e: On a nonpolar column, alkanes separate mainly by volatility (boiling point).
Pentane (bp 36 °C) spends the most time in the gas phase, so it elutes first; heptane (bp 98 °C) elutes last.
t: In GC, the more volatile compound (lower boiling point) usually comes out first.

q: Which method is best for separating pentane (bp 36 °C) from toluene (bp 111 °C)?
e: Both are neutral liquids, so acid–base extraction won't separate them, and neither is a solid to recrystallize.
Their boiling points differ by 75 °C (well over 25 °C), so simple distillation works: pentane distills first.

q: Acid chlorides must be stored away from moisture because they react with water. What are the products?
e: Water attacks the C=O, and Cl⁻ (a very good leaving group) leaves; the lost H⁺ and Cl⁻ make HCl.
RCOCl + H₂O → RCOOH + HCl. The fumes of HCl are why acid chlorides 'smoke' in moist air.

q: When an amide is hydrolyzed to a carboxylic acid and an amine, which bond is broken?
o: The bond between the carbonyl carbon and nitrogen
The C=O double bond of the carbonyl group
The bond between nitrogen and its hydrogen
The bond between the carbonyl carbon and the α-carbon
e: Hydrolysis is nucleophilic acyl substitution: water adds to C=O, then the nitrogen group leaves.
The acyl C–N bond breaks; the C=O is re-formed in the product carboxylic acid.

q: Why are β-lactam antibiotics (like penicillin) especially reactive toward bacterial enzymes?
o: The strained four-membered ring makes the amide unusually reactive
The fused benzene ring strongly activates the amide carbonyl
The strained ring makes the amide nitrogen strongly basic
Their large size lets them bind many enzyme sites at once
e: Ring strain and reduced amide resonance help them acylate the bacterial enzyme.

q: Saponification of a triglyceride with NaOH gives:
o: Glycerol and three fatty acid carboxylate salts
Glycerol and three fatty acid methyl esters
Glycerol and three neutral fatty acids
Three fatty alcohols and glyceric acid
e: These carboxylate salts are soaps.

q: N,N-Dimethylbenzamide, C₆H₅CON(CH₃)₂, is treated with LiAlH₄ and then water. What is the product?
e: LiAlH₄ reduces amides differently from esters: the C=O oxygen is removed, and the C–N bond stays.
C=O → CH₂, so the tertiary amide becomes the tertiary amine C₆H₅CH₂N(CH₃)₂.
t: LiAlH₄ + amide keeps the nitrogen: C=O simply becomes CH₂.

q: Which general mechanism characterizes reactions of many acyl chlorides with nucleophiles?
e: Nucleophilic addition to the carbonyl is followed by elimination of a leaving group.
w: The carbonyl carbon is trigonal, not SN2.

q: Transesterification is:
o: Exchanging an ester's alkoxy group for that of a different alcohol
Hydrolyzing an ester into a carboxylic acid and an alcohol
Converting an ester into an amide by reaction with an amine
Reducing an ester to two alcohols using LiAlH₄
e: Biodiesel is made this way from fats and methanol.

q: A lactam is a cyclic version of which functional group?
e: In a lactam, the N–C(=O) unit is part of a ring, so it is a cyclic amide.
A cyclic ester is a lactone instead.
t: LactONE has an extra Oxygen in the ring; lactAM has an AMide nitrogen.

q: Why are acid anhydrides more reactive toward nucleophiles than esters?
o: A carboxylate leaves more easily than an alkoxide does
Anhydride carbonyls are less polarized than ester carbonyls
An alkoxide leaves more easily than a carboxylate does
Esters are sterically more crowded at the carbonyl carbon
e: Leaving-group ability follows conjugate-acid strength: RCOO⁻ comes from RCOOH (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 5); RO⁻ comes from ROH (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16).
Also, the central oxygen shares its lone pairs between two carbonyls, so each C=O gets less resonance donation and stays more electrophilic.

q: Reducing an amide with LiAlH₄ gives:
e: The C=O becomes CH₂, keeping the nitrogen.

q: Which product forms when acetic anhydride reacts with ethanol?
e: One acetyl group transfers to ethanol; the other leaves as acetic acid.

q: When acetic anhydride transfers an acetyl group to a nucleophile, which species leaves from the tetrahedral intermediate?
e: Acetic anhydride is CH₃CO–O–COCH₃. After a nucleophile adds to one C=O, the C–O bond to the other acyl group breaks.
The leaving group is acetate, a resonance-stabilized, weak base, so it leaves easily.
t: Anhydrides are 'half-acid chlorides': one acyl group is delivered, the other leaves as a carboxylate.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃?
e: Number from the end giving –OH the lowest number: C2.

q: Which name matches the substituent –CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃?
e: The group is an unbranched 4-carbon chain.
It attaches through C2 of that chain (the CH), so it is butan-2-yl, also called sec-butyl.
t: iso = branch at the far end; sec = attached at a secondary carbon; tert = attached at a tertiary carbon.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CHBrCH₂CHClCH₃?
e: Both numbering directions give locants {2, 4}: a tie.
Break the tie alphabetically: bromo comes first, so Br gets the lower number (C2).
w: Halogens are on C2 and C4.

q: Which suffix is used when a –C≡N group is the principal group and its carbon is counted in the main chain?
e: A –C≡N group is a nitrile.
With the nitrile carbon counted in the chain, add -nitrile to the alkane name: CH₃CN is ethanenitrile.
-carbonitrile is used only when the CN carbon is NOT counted in the chain or ring (e.g., cyclohexanecarbonitrile).

q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₃?
e: Longest chain: 4 carbons (butane).
A methyl branch sits on C2 (number from the end closer to the branch).

q: In an ester's IUPAC name, which ending replaces the '-oic acid' ending of the parent carboxylic acid?
e: Esters are named as two words: the alkyl group from the alcohol, then the acid name with -oic acid changed to -oate.
Example: CH₃COOCH₃ is methyl ethanoate.
t: -oyl names an acyl group (ethanoyl = CH₃CO–), as in ethanoyl chloride.

q: What is the common name of propan-2-ol?
e: The –OH is on the middle carbon of a 3-carbon chain.

q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH₃CH₂)₂NH?
e: In a secondary amine, the larger (or either identical) alkyl group is the parent: ethanamine.
The other group on nitrogen gets the locant N → N-ethylethanamine (common name diethylamine).
An amide would need a C=O.

q: What is the IUPAC name of HOCH₂CH₂OH?
e: Two –OH groups on a two-carbon chain (common name: ethylene glycol).

q: On a benzene ring, the prefix meta- (m-) indicates two substituents at which positions?
e: ortho = 1,2 (adjacent); meta = 1,3 (one carbon between); para = 1,4 (directly across).
These prefixes apply only to disubstituted rings.
t: O-M-P goes 2-3-4: ortho 1,2; meta 1,3; para 1,4.

q: An unsubstituted ring of five carbons joined only by single bonds is named:
e: Add cyclo- in front of the alkane name for the number of ring carbons: 5 → cyclopentane.
Pentane is the open chain (C₅H₁₂); the ring has two fewer H atoms (C₅H₁₀).

q: What is the common name of propanone?
e: CH₃COCH₃ is the simplest ketone.

q: Breaking a C=C bond completely takes about 610 kJ mol⁻¹, while breaking a C–C single bond takes about 350 kJ mol⁻¹. What do these values suggest about the π bond?
o: It is weaker than the σ bond, about 260 kJ mol⁻¹
It is stronger than the σ bond, about 610 kJ mol⁻¹
It equals the σ bond, about 305 kJ mol⁻¹ each
It is stronger than the σ bond, about 350 kJ mol⁻¹
e: A C=C is one σ plus one π bond, so π ≈ 610 − 350 = 260 kJ mol⁻¹.
260 < 350: side-by-side p overlap is weaker than head-on σ overlap, which is why π bonds are the reactive part of alkenes.

q: Acrolein, CH₂=CH–CHO, has a resonance form in which the C=C and C=O electrons both shift. Besides the carbonyl carbon, which atom carries a partial + charge as a result?
o: The hydrogen on the aldehyde carbon
e: Push the C=O π electrons onto O (O⁻), then move the C=C π electrons toward the carbonyl carbon.
That leaves the end CH₂ carbon with a + charge: ⁺CH₂–CH=CH–O⁻.
So the β-carbon is electrophilic, which is why nucleophiles can add there.

q: Lab techs estimate protein concentration from absorbance at 280 nm. Which structural feature is mainly responsible for this absorbance?
o: Conjugated aromatic rings of Trp and Tyr side chains
The C=O π bonds found in every peptide bond
The sp³ C–H bonds of Leu and Val side chains
Hydrogen bonds between backbone N–H and C=O
e: Isolated π bonds (like a peptide C=O) absorb below about 230 nm; sp³ C–H bonds absorb only in the far UV.
The larger conjugated π systems of tryptophan's indole and tyrosine's phenol have smaller HOMO–LUMO gaps and absorb near 280 nm.
t: More conjugation → smaller energy gap → longer wavelength absorbed.

q: Which pair are NOT resonance structures of each other?
o: Acetone and its enol form, prop-1-en-2-ol
The two Kekulé structures of benzene
Acetate drawn with − on either oxygen
Allyl cation drawn with + on either end
e: Resonance structures differ only in where electrons are drawn; every atom stays put.
Going from acetone to its enol moves a hydrogen atom, so they are tautomers: two different real compounds.
t: If an atom moves, it's not resonance.

q: What is the hybridization of the nitrogen in an amide (R–CONH₂)?
o: sp², because its lone pair is in resonance with the C=O
sp³, because it has three σ bonds plus one lone pair
sp, because the C–N bond has partial triple-bond character
sp³d, because N expands its octet to form the C–N π bond
e: The N lone pair delocalizes into the C=O, making the amide group planar.
This planarity is why peptide bonds don't rotate freely.

q: In methyl vinyl ether, CH₂=CH–O–CH₃, oxygen's lone pair is conjugated with the C=C. Which carbon becomes electron-rich (δ−) as a result?
o: The CH carbon bonded to O
e: Draw the resonance form: an O lone pair forms a C=O⁺ π bond, pushing the C=C electrons onto the end carbon: ⁻CH₂–CH=O⁺–CH₃.
So the terminal carbon is δ− (nucleophilic) — the opposite of an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl, where the end carbon is δ+.
t: Lone-pair donors (O, N) push electron density to the far end of an attached C=C.

q: What is the hybridization of the oxygen atom in methanol (CH₃OH)?
e: Oxygen has 2 bonds (to C and H) and 2 lone pairs: 4 electron groups.
Four electron groups means sp³ (a bent shape, about 109°).

q: Why is cyclopropane far more strained than cyclohexane?
o: Its C–C–C angles are 60°, far from the ideal 109.5°
Its carbons are sp², which forces 120° angles
Its chair form puts every hydrogen axial
Its C–C bonds are π bonds, which are weaker
e: Each carbon in cyclopropane is sp³-like and 'wants' 109.5°.
A triangle forces 60° angles, so the orbitals overlap poorly (bent bonds). This angle strain, plus eclipsed H's, makes cyclopropane reactive. Cyclohexane's chair is nearly strain-free.

q: Histidine's imidazole side chain has two nitrogens. Why is only one of them basic?
o: One N's lone pair is in the aromatic π system; the other's is free
One N is permanently protonated, so only the other can take H⁺
One N is sp³ and the other sp², and sp³ lone pairs aren't basic
The two N atoms share one lone pair, so only one can be protonated
e: The pyridine-like N can be protonated (pKa about 6), making histidine useful in enzyme active sites.

q: What is the hybridization of the nitrogen atom in a nitrile (R–C≡N)?
e: The nitrile N has two electron domains: the C≡N bond and one lone pair.
Two domains → sp, linear geometry (C–C≡N is 180°).

q: Cycloocta-1,3,5,7-tetraene has 8 π electrons but is NOT strongly destabilized the way cyclobutadiene is. Why?
o: It folds into a tub, so π overlap around the ring breaks
8 electrons fit 4n + 2, so it is actually aromatic
Its carbons are sp³, so it has no π bonds
It is planar, but its large ring has no strain
e: A planar, fully conjugated ring with 8 π electrons (4n, n = 2) would be antiaromatic.
Cyclooctatetraene avoids this by bending into a tub shape: its C=C bonds are no longer conjugated around the ring, so it behaves as an ordinary (nonaromatic) polyene.
t: Antiaromaticity can only happen if the ring stays flat; big rings can pucker to escape it.

q: What is the geometry of the methyl anion, :CH₃⁻?
e: The carbon has three bonds and one lone pair: four electron domains → sp³.
With one domain a lone pair, the shape is trigonal pyramidal; :CH₃⁻ is isoelectronic with NH₃.

q: 2-Bromobutane is heated with sodium ethoxide in ethanol. What is the major product?
e: A strong, unhindered base with a 2° halide and heat favors E2.
Zaitsev: the more substituted alkene (but-2-ene) is favored over but-1-ene.
The trans isomer is favored over cis because its methyls are kept apart.

q: Which solvent best favors SN2 reactions?
o: A polar aprotic solvent, like acetone or DMSO
A polar protic solvent, like water or methanol
A nonpolar solvent, like hexane or toluene
A protic acidic solvent, like acetic acid
e: Polar aprotic solvents don't hydrogen bond to the nucleophile, so it stays reactive.

q: An SN2 reaction at a chiral carbon gives:
e: Backside attack flips the molecule like an umbrella in the wind.

q: A carbon atom with only three bonds, six valence electrons and a positive charge is a:
e: A carbocation has 3 bonds, an empty p orbital and a + charge.
A carbanion has 3 bonds + a lone pair (− charge); a radical has 7 electrons; a carbene is neutral with only 2 bonds.

q: Which compound reacts fastest by SN1 in aqueous ethanol?
e: SN1 rate tracks the stability of the carbocation formed in the slow step.
PhC(CH₃)₂⁺ is tertiary AND benzylic: the + charge spreads into the ring by resonance, so it forms fastest.
A phenyl cation (from bromobenzene) is extremely unstable, so bromobenzene doesn't react by SN1.

q: Bromobenzene is stirred with NaOH in water at 25 °C. What happens?
o: No reaction occurs at the ring C–Br bond
SN2 gives phenol, with inversion at C1
SN1 gives phenol via a phenyl cation
E2 gives cyclohexene as the main product
e: SN2 fails: backside attack would require the nucleophile to approach through the ring, and the sp² C–Br bond is strong.
SN1 fails: a phenyl cation is very unstable because its empty orbital lies in the ring plane, so the ring's π system can't stabilize it.
t: Aryl and vinyl halides don't do SN1 or SN2.

q: A carbocation rearranges from secondary to tertiary by a 1,2-hydride shift. Why?
o: The tertiary carbocation is more stable
e: Rearrangements are common in SN1 and E1 reactions.

q: In a polar protic solvent such as methanol, which halide ion is the strongest nucleophile?
e: Protic solvents hydrogen-bond strongly to small, charge-dense anions like F⁻, surrounding and slowing them.
I⁻ is large and polarizable, so it is the least tied up and the most nucleophilic in protic solvents.
t: Protic: I⁻ best. Aprotic: F⁻ best. The solvent flips the order.

q: A good leaving group is usually:
o: A weak base that is stable on its own
e: Example: I⁻, Br⁻, Cl⁻, water and tosylate (TsO⁻) are good leaving groups; OH⁻ is poor.

q: An oxidation in organic chemistry usually involves:
o: Gaining bonds to oxygen or losing bonds to hydrogen
Gaining bonds to hydrogen or losing bonds to oxygen
Gaining bonds to carbon or losing bonds to halogen
Adding water across a C=C bond with an acid catalyst
e: Example: alcohol → aldehyde is an oxidation.

q: An SN1 reaction has k = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. What is the initial rate when [R–Cl] = 0.50 M and the nucleophile concentration is 2.0 M?
e: SN1: rate = k[R–Cl]; the nucleophile is not in the rate law.
t: 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ is the trap answer that wrongly multiplies by [Nu] = 2.0 M.

q: For E2 in a cyclohexane chair, the H and leaving group must be anti-periplanar. In the chair, this means both must be:
o: Axial, on adjacent carbons and opposite faces
Equatorial, on adjacent carbons and the same face
Axial, on adjacent carbons and the same face
Equatorial, on adjacent carbons and opposite faces
e: Anti-periplanar means the H–C–C–LG atoms lie in one plane with the H and LG 180° apart.
On adjacent ring carbons, only two axial bonds (one up, one down: trans-diaxial) line up this way.
t: Ring E2 needs trans-diaxial H and LG.

q: As the carbon chain of a straight-chain alcohol gets longer (methanol → octan-1-ol), its solubility in water:
e: Every alcohol has one –OH that H-bonds with water.
A longer chain adds more nonpolar surface that water cannot H-bond to, so solubility drops.

q: Glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol) is used in many medicines and lotions. Why is it so water-soluble?
o: Its three –OH groups form many hydrogen bonds with water
It ionizes in water to give a glycerate anion and H⁺
Its polar C–H bonds interact strongly with water's dipoles
Its three ester groups accept hydrogen bonds from water
e: Small molecules with several –OH groups are highly water-soluble.

q: Oxidizing ethanol with PCC gives:
e: PCC stops at the aldehyde.

q: In a vicinal diol such as ethane-1,2-diol, where are the two –OH groups?
o: On carbons at opposite chain ends
On carbons separated by one CH₂
e: Vicinal (from the Latin for 'neighbor') means on neighboring carbons: a 1,2-diol.
Two –OH groups on the same carbon make a geminal diol (a carbonyl hydrate).
t: Geminal = twins on one carbon; vicinal = next-door neighbors.

q: In the body, ethanol is oxidized first to:
e: Alcohol dehydrogenase: ethanol → acetaldehyde (toxic, causes hangover symptoms).
Aldehyde dehydrogenase then makes acetate.

q: Why do alcohols have higher boiling points than alkanes of similar size?
e: Ethanol boils at 78 °C; propane (similar mass) at −42 °C.

q: Why does the Williamson ether synthesis fail with tertiary alkyl halides?
o: The alkoxide acts as a base, causing E2 elimination instead
The alkoxide is too weak a nucleophile to attack tertiary carbon
Tertiary carbocations are too unstable to form in the solvent
Tertiary ethers are unstable and decompose as soon as they form
e: Alkoxides are strong bases; hindered substrates favor E2.

q: Which alcohol is most easily dehydrated by acid?
e: Dehydration goes through a carbocation (E1); tertiary cations form most easily.

q: Oxidizing a secondary alcohol gives:
e: Secondary alcohols have one H on the carbinol carbon to remove.

q: (S)-Butan-2-ol is treated with TsCl and pyridine. What is the configuration at the stereocenter of the tosylate that forms?
o: S, because the C–O bond is not broken
R, because the oxygen is attacked from the back
Racemic, because a carbocation forms first
R, because OTs changes the priority order
e: The alcohol's oxygen attacks the sulfur of TsCl; only the O–H bond breaks.
The C–O bond to the stereocenter is untouched, so its arrangement is retained, and O still has top priority, so the label stays S.
Inversion happens only later, if a nucleophile does SN2 on the tosylate.

q: Which alcohol gives only ONE alkene product when dehydrated with acid (counting cis/trans isomers as different products)?
e: Cyclohexanol's carbocation is symmetric: losing H⁺ from either neighbor gives the same cyclohexene.
Butan-2-ol and pentan-2-ol give a 1-ene plus cis- and trans-2-enes.
2-Methylbutan-2-ol gives both 2-methylbut-2-ene and 2-methylbut-1-ene.

q: Hydroquinone (benzene-1,4-diol) is gently oxidized. What is the product?
e: Each –OH loses its H (2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻ in total), and both oxygens become C=O.
The product is a quinone; the change is reversible.
Ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) uses this same quinone ⇌ hydroquinone redox to carry electrons in the ETC.

q: What is the main driving force of the Wittig reaction?
o: Formation of the very strong P=O bond in Ph₃P=O
Formation of a carbocation intermediate on carbon
Release of a gas that bubbles out of solution
Formation of an aromatic ring in the alkene product
e: The ylide carbon attacks the C=O, giving a four-membered ring containing C, C, P and O (an oxaphosphetane).
The ring falls apart to the alkene plus triphenylphosphine oxide; the P=O bond (over 500 kJ mol⁻¹) is so strong that this step is strongly downhill.

q: Which compound is a ketone?
e: A ketone's carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbons.
Cyclohexanone's C=O carbon is bonded to two ring carbons. Butanal has an H on its carbonyl carbon (aldehyde); methyl acetate has an O (ester) and acetamide an N (amide).

q: Why are aldehydes easily oxidized to carboxylic acids, while ketones resist oxidation?
o: An aldehyde has an H on its carbonyl carbon
An aldehyde has a lone pair on its carbonyl carbon
A ketone's oxygen has a full positive charge
e: Oxidizing R–CHO to R–COOH replaces the carbonyl C–H with C–OH.
A ketone's carbonyl carbon has two C–C bonds; oxidizing it would require breaking a C–C bond.

q: 0.050 mol of propanal reacts completely with excess Tollens' reagent, [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺. What mass of silver is deposited? (Ag = 108 g mol⁻¹)
e: RCHO → RCOO⁻ is a 2-electron oxidation, and each Ag⁺ accepts 1 electron, so 2 Ag form per aldehyde.

q: Pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B₆) forms an imine with amino acids during transamination. Which functional group on PLP makes this possible?
e: The aldehyde reacts with the amino acid's amine to form a Schiff base.

q: When a primary amine reacts with a ketone to form an imine, which intermediate forms just before water is lost?
e: The amine adds to the C=O carbon, and proton transfers give a carbinolamine (hemiaminal).
Acid protonates its –OH, water leaves, and loss of N–H gives the C=N bond.

q: An aldehyde is converted to an alkene using a phosphorus ylide. This reaction is the:
e: The C=O becomes a C=C.

q: Acetaldehyde is treated with excess methanol and a trace of acid. What is the final product?
e: One methanol adds to give the hemiacetal, CH₃CH(OH)OCH₃.
With excess alcohol and acid, the –OH is replaced by a second –OCH₃ (water leaves), giving the acetal 1,1-dimethoxyethane.

q: Why does triethylamine, (CH₃CH₂)₃N, form neither an imine nor an enamine with acetone?
o: Its nitrogen has no H to lose after adding
It is too weakly basic to attack any C=O
It is fully protonated at every pH
Its nitrogen has no lone pair to donate
e: Imines need an N with two H's (1° amine); enamines need an N with one H (2° amine).
After a 3° amine adds, the nitrogen is positive with no H to remove, so no stable neutral product forms and the addition reverses.

q: The imine (CH₃)₂C=N–CH₂CH₃ is hydrolyzed in aqueous acid. Which products form?
e: Hydrolysis reverses imine formation: water adds across C=N, and the C–N bond breaks.
The carbon side becomes a C=O: (CH₃)₂C=O, acetone.
The nitrogen side becomes the amine: H₂N–CH₂CH₃, ethylamine.

q: Aldehydes and ketones react with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNP) to give a yellow-orange solid. What type of compound forms?
o: A hydrazone, with a C=N–NH–Ar group
A hemiacetal, with a C(OH)–OR group
An enamine, with a C=C–NR₂ group
A cyanohydrin, with a C(OH)–CN group
e: The –NH₂ end of the hydrazine adds to the C=O, then water is lost, just as in imine formation.
The product, R₂C=N–NH–C₆H₃(NO₂)₂, is a 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone, a colored solid.
t: 2,4-DNP is positive for any aldehyde or ketone; it doesn't tell the two apart.

q: Glucose cyclizes when its C5 –OH attacks its C1 aldehyde. What functional group forms?
e: One –OH and one –OR on the same carbon: a hemiacetal.

q: Racemization at an α-carbon stereocenter can happen in acid or base. Why?
o: Forming the planar enol or enolate erases the stereochemistry
Forming a planar carbocation at the α-carbon erases it
Repeated SN2 attack by water inverts the α-carbon
Reduction of the carbonyl makes the α-carbon achiral
e: Re-protonation can occur on either face.

q: An enolate is formed when a base removes:
e: The negative charge is shared between the α-carbon and oxygen.

q: Pentane-2,4-dione (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 9) is mixed with sodium ethoxide (ethanol pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16). About what is the equilibrium constant for the proton transfer?
e: K = 10<sup>(pK<sub>a</sub> of product acid − pK<sub>a</sub> of reactant acid)</sup> = 10<sup>(16 − 9)</sup> = 10<sup>7</sup>.
The equilibrium lies far toward the enolate and ethanol, so ethoxide deprotonates the dione essentially completely.
t: Proton transfer favors the side with the weaker acid (the higher pK<sub>a</sub>).

q: For most simple ketones, which tautomer is favored?
e: The C=O bond is much stronger than C=C.

q: Acetoacetic acid (a ketone body) spontaneously decarboxylates to form:
e: CH₃COCH₂COOH → CH₃COCH₃ + CO₂

q: Acetone is heated with NaOH so that the aldol product dehydrates. What is the main product?
e: The acetone enolate (CH₂⁻) attacks another acetone: (CH₃)₂C(OH)–CH₂–CO–CH₃.
Heat removes water, giving a C=C conjugated with the C=O: (CH₃)₂C=CH–CO–CH₃.
4-Hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one is the addition product before dehydration.

q: The Claisen condensation joins two esters to form a:
e: It's the ester version of the aldol reaction.

q: Fatty acid synthase builds fatty acids by joining acetyl and malonyl units with loss of CO₂. Which pair of reactions does this combine?
e: Decarboxylating malonyl drives the C–C bond-forming condensation.

q: Propanal is treated with dilute NaOH at low temperature (no dehydration). What is the aldol addition product?
e: The enolate forms at C2 of propanal (the CH₂ next to C=O).
C2 attacks C1 of a second propanal: CH₃CH₂–CH(OH)–CH(CH₃)–CHO.
Longest chain with CHO: 5 carbons, OH on C3, methyl on C2.
t: The α-carbon becomes the branch point, so self-aldols of aldehydes other than acetaldehyde always give a branch at C2.

q: In the last step of each β-oxidation cycle, thiolase uses CoA–SH to split a 3-ketoacyl-CoA into acetyl-CoA and an acyl-CoA two carbons shorter. This cleavage is the reverse of which reaction?
e: A Claisen condensation joins an ester (or thioester) enolate to another (thio)ester, giving a β-keto (thio)ester.
Thiolase does the reverse: CoA–S⁻ attacks the ketone C=O of the β-keto thioester, and the enolate of acetyl-CoA leaves (a retro-Claisen).
In ketone-body synthesis the same chemistry runs forward, joining two acetyl-CoA into acetoacetyl-CoA.

q: Why can a ketone's stereocenter at the α-carbon be lost over time in a basic drug formulation?
o: Enolate formation lets the α-stereocenter racemize
Base hydrolyzes the ketone into a carboxylate salt
Hydroxide attacks the α-carbon by SN2, inverting it
Base reduces the ketone to an achiral alcohol
e: Formulations may be buffered to slow this process.

q: In a Claisen condensation of ethyl acetate, why is sodium ethoxide used instead of sodium hydroxide?
o: NaOH would hydrolyze the ester to a carboxylate
NaOH is too weak to form any enolate
Ethoxide is a stronger base than LDA
Ethoxide reacts with the ester irreversibly
e: Hydroxide attacks the ester C=O, giving acetate (saponification), which can't do a Claisen.
Ethoxide can also attack the ester, but that only swaps –OEt for –OEt, so nothing is lost.
Rule: match the alkoxide base to the ester's alkoxy group.

q: 4-Hydroxybutanoic acid forms a lactone easily when warmed with acid, but 3-hydroxypropanoic acid does not. Why?
o: Its lactone would be a strained four-membered ring
It has no –OH group to attack the carboxyl carbon
Its –OH is too acidic to act as a nucleophile
Its lactone would be a strained three-membered ring
e: Count ring atoms: the –OH oxygen, the carbons in between, and the carboxyl carbon.
4-Hydroxybutanoic acid gives a five-membered ring (γ-butyrolactone), which is almost strain-free.
3-Hydroxypropanoic acid would give a four-membered β-lactone, which is highly strained, so it doesn't form easily.

q: Acetic acid + ethanol (with H₂SO₄) gives which ester?
e: Alkyl group from the alcohol (ethyl) + acid part (acetate).

q: Benzoic acid is treated with SOCl₂, and the product is then added to excess NH₃. What is the final product?
e: SOCl₂ converts –COOH into the very reactive acid chloride, C₆H₅COCl.
NH₃ attacks the acid chloride C=O and Cl⁻ leaves, giving the amide (extra NH₃ absorbs the HCl).
Mixing benzoic acid with NH₃ directly would only give the ammonium salt.

q: Many drugs that contain a carboxylic acid are given as ethyl ester prodrugs (for example, the ACE inhibitor enalapril). How does this most likely improve oral absorption?
o: Masking one –COOH makes it less charged; esterases free the acid
The ester is more ionized at pH 7.4, so it dissolves better
Esters bind the drug target more strongly than acids
The ester cannot be hydrolyzed, so it lasts longer
e: At intestinal and blood pH, a –COOH (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 4) is mostly ionized and crosses lipid membranes poorly.
Esterifying the –COOH removes one negative charge, so the molecule is less polar and more lipophilic.
After absorption, esterase enzymes hydrolyze it back to the active carboxylic acid.

q: Freezing-point depression in benzene gives an apparent molar mass of about 120 g mol⁻¹ for acetic acid (true value 60 g mol⁻¹). What explains this?
o: Acetic acid forms hydrogen-bonded dimers in benzene
Acetic acid ionizes completely in benzene
Benzene reacts with acetic acid to form an ester
Acetic acid's molar mass doubles when it freezes
e: Colligative properties count particles.
In a nonpolar solvent, two acid molecules pair up through two O–H···O=C hydrogen bonds.
Half as many particles makes the apparent molar mass about 2 × 60 = 120 g mol⁻¹.

q: A student tries to make terephthalic acid (benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid) by treating 4-bromobenzoic acid with Mg in ether, then CO₂, then H₃O⁺. Mostly benzoic acid is recovered. What went wrong?
o: Each Grignard formed was protonated by a –COOH group
CO₂ added twice to the same Grignard carbon atom
The Grignard reagent attacked the ether solvent instead
The ring bromine was replaced by an –OH group in workup
e: An aryl Grignard carbon is extremely basic (its conjugate acid, benzene, has pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 43).
As soon as Ar–MgBr forms, it removes an acidic –COOH proton (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 4), turning the C–Mg carbon into C–H. After workup, that molecule is benzoic acid.
Grignard reagents can't be made or used in the presence of O–H groups such as acids, alcohols or water.

q: A carboxylic acid and a primary amine are mixed at room temperature. What mainly forms?
o: An amide, with loss of water
An ester, with loss of ammonia
An imine, with loss of water
e: The fastest reaction is acid–base: RCOOH + R′NH₂ → RCOO⁻ ⁺H₃NR′.
The carboxylate is a poor electrophile, so amide formation requires strong heating or an activating agent (e.g., converting to an acid chloride, or DCC).
t: Acid + amine at room temperature = salt, not amide.

q: How does distance affect the acid-strengthening effect of a chlorine substituent?
o: The closer the Cl is to the carboxyl group, the stronger the effect
The farther the Cl is from the carboxyl group, the stronger the effect
The effect is the same at every position along the carbon chain
A nearby Cl weakens the acid, while a distant Cl strengthens it
e: The inductive effect falls off quickly with distance.

q: Formic acid (HCOOH, pK<sub>a</sub> 3.75) is a stronger acid than acetic acid (CH₃COOH, pK<sub>a</sub> 4.76). Why?
o: The CH₃ group donates electron density, destabilizing acetate
Formic acid has more resonance forms than acetic acid
The CH₃ group withdraws electron density from the O–H
Formate is stabilized by hydrogen bonding to its C–H
e: Alkyl groups are weakly electron-donating.
Pushing electron density toward an already-negative carboxylate destabilizes it, so acetic acid ionizes less.

q: Which haloacetic acid is the strongest acid?
e: All four have one halogen on the α-carbon, so the difference is electronegativity.
F is the most electronegative, so it withdraws the most electron density and best stabilizes the carboxylate.

q: Acetic acid reacts with ethanol whose oxygen is labeled with ¹⁸O, using an acid catalyst. Where does the ¹⁸O end up?
o: In the ester, as the O bonded to the ethyl group
Split evenly between the ester and water
e: The alcohol's oxygen attacks the protonated acid's carbonyl carbon and stays bonded to ethyl.
The water that leaves comes from the acid's original –OH.
So the label appears as CH₃CO–¹⁸O–CH₂CH₃.
t: In Fischer esterification, the acid loses OH and the alcohol loses H.

q: Which sequence converts 1-bromobutane into pentanoic acid?
o: NaCN in DMSO, then H₃O⁺ with heat
Mg in ether, then H₂C=O, then H₃O⁺
NaOH(aq), then hot KMnO₄, then H₃O⁺
Mg in ether, then H₂O as workup
e: Pentanoic acid (C₅) has one carbon more than 1-bromobutane (C₄), so the new COOH carbon must be added.
CN⁻ displaces Br⁻ (SN2) to give CH₃(CH₂)₃CN; hot aqueous acid then hydrolyzes C≡N to COOH: CH₃(CH₂)₃COOH.
Mg/H₂C=O gives pentan-1-ol (an alcohol), NaOH then KMnO₄ gives butanoic acid (no added carbon), and Mg then H₂O gives butane.

q: A kinase phosphorylates a serine side chain (–CH₂OH → –CH₂OPO₃H₂, whose second pK<sub>a</sub> is about 6). At pH 7.4, how does this change the charge at that site?
e: The serine –OH is neutral at pH 7.4.
A phosphate monoester has two acidic O–H groups: pK<sub>a1</sub> ≈ 1–2 (fully ionized) and pK<sub>a2</sub> ≈ 6. At pH 7.4, about 1.4 units above pK<sub>a2</sub>, about 96% is the dianion.
t: Adding a phosphate adds roughly two negative charges, which is why phosphorylation can switch protein shape so strongly.

q: Amphetamine is a basic drug. Making the urine more acidic speeds up its excretion. Why?
o: More drug is protonated (charged) in acidic urine, so less is reabsorbed
More drug is neutral in acidic urine, so it is filtered out faster
More drug is deprotonated in acidic urine, so less is reabsorbed
Acidic urine hydrolyzes the amine into easily excreted fragments
e: Charged molecules are 'trapped' in urine (ion trapping).

q: At pH 7.4, a typical primary amine (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 10.6) exists mainly as:
o: A roughly 50:50 mix of R–NH₂ and R–NH₃⁺
e: pH below pKa → protonated.

q: How many water molecules are released when 4 amino acids join to form a tetrapeptide?
e: Each peptide bond releases one water (condensation).

q: In terpene biosynthesis, dimethylallyl diphosphate, (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₂–OPP, loses its diphosphate group to form an allylic carbocation. Why is diphosphate such a good leaving group here?
o: As an anion it is a weak base, stabilized by resonance and Mg²⁺
It is a strong base, so it pulls away from carbon with great force
It is neutral when it leaves, so no charge has to be stabilized
It forms a C=O bond as it leaves, releasing a great deal of energy
e: Good leaving groups are weak bases. Diphosphate's negative charges are spread over several oxygens by resonance.
In enzymes, bound Mg²⁺ ions further neutralize that charge. The allylic cation left behind is also resonance-stabilized.

q: Acetylating aniline gives acetanilide, C₆H₅NHCOCH₃. How does the basicity of its nitrogen compare with that of aniline?
o: Much less basic, since the lone pair is also shared with C=O
Much more basic, since the acetyl group donates electrons
About the same, since the N still has a lone pair
More basic, since the N now has only one H attached
e: In acetanilide, the N lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl (amide resonance) as well as the ring.
Amide nitrogens are essentially non-basic, so acetylation is a way to 'tame' a reactive amine.

q: Why is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane a poor choice for making tert-butylamine by the Gabriel synthesis?
o: Tertiary halides can't undergo SN2, so elimination dominates
Tertiary halides are too unreactive to give any product
The amine product would be alkylated two more times
Tertiary carbocations cannot form, so no reaction occurs
e: The Gabriel synthesis needs SN2 attack by the bulky phthalimide anion.
A tertiary carbon is too hindered for SN2; the basic anion removes a β-H instead (E2), giving 2-methylpropene.
t: SN2-based amine syntheses (Gabriel, azide) work best on methyl and primary halides.

q: Strong acids protonate amides on the carbonyl oxygen rather than on nitrogen. Why?
o: O-protonation keeps the resonance, spreading + over O, C and N
Oxygen is less electronegative than nitrogen, so it is more basic
Nitrogen in an amide has no lone pair left to share at all
Protonating oxygen breaks the C–N bond, giving a stable product
e: Protonating N would take its lone pair out of resonance and leave the + charge stuck on N.
Protonating O gives a cation where the N lone pair still donates: [C=OH⁺ ↔ C(OH)=N⁺], so the charge is delocalized and the ion is more stable.
t: Amides protonate on O, not N; the same resonance that makes them non-basic decides where H⁺ goes.

q: The second pK<sub>a</sub> of phosphoric acid (H₂PO₄⁻ ⇌ HPO₄²⁻ + H⁺) is about 7.2. In a phosphate buffer at pH 6.2, what is the ratio [HPO₄²⁻] : [H₂PO₄⁻]?
e: log([HPO₄²⁻]/[H₂PO₄⁻]) = pH − pK<sub>a</sub> = 6.2 − 7.2 = −1
Ratio = 10⁻¹, or 1 : 10, so the more protonated H₂PO₄⁻ dominates.

q: ATP stores energy in its:
e: Two phosphoanhydride bonds link its three phosphates.

q: How is CH₃CONHCH₃ (N-methylacetamide) classified?
e: Amides are classified by how many carbon groups sit on nitrogen: RCONH₂ (1°), RCONHR′ (2°), RCONR′₂ (3°).
Here N carries one H and one CH₃, so it is a secondary amide. It is not an amine, because N is bonded to a C=O.

q: What is the main reason DNA's phosphate backbone resists hydrolysis much better than RNA's?
o: DNA lacks the 2′-OH that can attack the neighboring phosphate
DNA's 2′-OH hydrogen bonds to and shields the neighboring phosphate
DNA's thymine methyl groups sterically shield each phosphate
DNA has fewer phosphate groups per nucleotide than RNA has
e: RNA's 2′-OH acts as an internal nucleophile, cleaving the backbone.

q: β-Carotene, with 11 conjugated C=C bonds, looks orange. In which part of the visible spectrum does it absorb most strongly?
e: The color we see is the light that is NOT absorbed (the complementary color).
Orange appears when blue (about 450–480 nm) is absorbed. Long conjugation lowers the π → π* energy gap enough to absorb visible light.
t: Seen color is the complement of the absorbed color: absorbs blue → looks orange.

q: Which ¹³C NMR feature distinguishes a ketone carbonyl carbon?
e: Carbonyl carbons are strongly deshielded (about 160–220 ppm).

q: How many degrees of unsaturation (rings + π bonds) does C₆H₁₀O have?
e: Oxygen doesn't change the count, so ignore it.
Cyclohexanone (1 ring + 1 C=O) is one example.

q: By the n + 1 rule, a hydrogen with 2 equivalent neighboring hydrogens appears as a:
e: n + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3 peaks.

q: A compound C₃H₆O shows a ¹H NMR triplet (3 H, ~1.1 ppm), a multiplet (2 H, ~2.4 ppm) and a triplet (1 H, ~9.8 ppm). Which structure fits best?
e: The ~9.8 ppm signal is an aldehyde H.
It is split by the neighboring CH₂ (small coupling).

q: Which compound's C=O stretch appears at the highest wavenumber?
e: Cl withdraws electrons inductively and donates little by resonance, so the C=O stays short and stiff (about 1800 cm⁻¹).

Ester (about 1740) > ketone (about 1715): the ester oxygen withdraws electrons inductively more than it donates by resonance. Amide (about 1650–1690 cm⁻¹) is lowest because nitrogen's strong resonance donation gives the C=O the most single-bond character.
t: Acid chloride (~1800) > ester (~1740) > ketone (~1715) > amide (~1650–1690): inductive withdrawal raises the C=O frequency, and resonance donation (strongest from N) lowers it.

q: Which IR absorption corresponds to the highest-energy bond vibration?
e: Energy is proportional to wavenumber: E = hcν̃.
The largest wavenumber, 3300 cm⁻¹ (an O–H or N–H stretch region), is the highest energy.

q: Amide C=O stretches (about 1650–1690 cm⁻¹) appear at lower wavenumbers than ketone C=O stretches (about 1715 cm⁻¹). Why?
o: N lone-pair resonance gives the C=O partial single-bond character
Amides are heavier, so all of their bonds vibrate more slowly
Hydrogen bonding is impossible in amides, weakening the C=O
The nitrogen withdraws electrons, strengthening the C=O bond
e: Stretching frequency rises with bond strength (a stiffer 'spring').
N donates its lone pair into the carbonyl (N–C=O ↔ N⁺=C–O⁻), so the C=O bond is weaker than a ketone's and absorbs at a lower wavenumber.

q: Each carbon atom has about a 1.1% chance of being ¹³C. A hydrocarbon's mass spectrum shows an M + 1 peak that is 6.6% as tall as its M⁺ peak. About how many carbon atoms does it contain?
e: Each carbon adds about 1.1% to the M + 1 / M ratio.
Number of C ≈ 6.6 ÷ 1.1 = 6 (for example, C₆H₁₄ or C₆H₁₂).

q: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis has a fruity odor on the breath. GC–MS of a breath sample shows a compound with M⁺ at m/z 58 and a base peak at m/z 43. Which compound fits?
e: Acetone, C₃H₆O: 3(12) + 6(1) + 16 = 58 ✓ (ethanol = 46, acetic acid = 60, acetaldehyde = 44).
Losing ·CH₃ (15) gives the stable acylium ion CH₃C≡O⁺ at m/z 43.
Acetone forms when the ketone body acetoacetate loses CO₂.

q: The mass spectra of many alcohols show a peak 18 units below the molecular ion (M − 18). What neutral loss does this represent?
e: Water, H₂O, has mass 2(1) + 16 = 18.
Alcohol radical cations often lose H₂O (dehydration), giving an M − 18 peak. Loss of ·OH or NH₃ would give M − 17; loss of CH₄ gives M − 16.

q: Aromatic ring hydrogens appear near:
e: The ring current deshields them.

q: Nicotine (shown) has two nitrogen atoms. When nicotine picks up one proton in water, which nitrogen is protonated?
o: The sp³ nitrogen in the five-membered ring
The sp² nitrogen in the six-membered aromatic ring
Neither; nicotine's nitrogens are not basic
Both equally, since they have the same pK<sub>a</sub>
e: The five-membered ring N is a tertiary alkylamine (sp³), conjugate-acid pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 8.
The pyridine-type N is sp² (more s character), pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 3, so it is much less basic. The first proton goes to the sp³ N.
t: Most basic N = the sp³ N whose lone pair is not tied up in resonance or an aromatic ring.

q: The table shows a compound's solubility in four solvents, cold and at the boiling point. Which solvent is best for recrystallizing it?
e: A good solvent dissolves a lot hot and very little cold.
Toluene: 15 g hot vs 0.4 g cold, so most of it crystallizes on cooling. Ethanol keeps too much dissolved cold (18 g); water and hexane barely dissolve it even hot.

q: The β-hydroxy ketone shown was made by an aldol addition. Which starting material(s) were used?
e: Break the bond between the α-carbon and the carbon bearing the –OH (the β-carbon).
CH₃CO–CH₂ | C(OH)(CH₃)₂: the left piece is acetone's enolate, and the right piece is an acetone C=O.
So two acetones combine to give 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one.

q: Compound Y (shown) contains a ketone and an acetal. A chemist wants to reduce the ketone's C=O all the way to CH₂ while keeping the acetal. Which conditions should be used?
o: NaBH₄ in methanol at room temperature
Aqueous H₃O⁺ with heat, then NaBH₄
e: Both Wolff–Kishner (basic) and Clemmensen (acidic) conditions convert C=O to CH₂.
Acetals survive base but are hydrolyzed by aqueous acid, so hot HCl would remove the acetal.
NaBH₄ only reduces C=O to CH–OH, not all the way to CH₂.
t: Acid-sensitive molecule: Wolff–Kishner. Base-sensitive molecule: Clemmensen.

q: 4-Phenylbutan-2-one (shown) is made by an acetoacetic ester synthesis: ethyl acetoacetate with NaOEt, then an alkyl halide, then H₃O⁺ and heat. Which alkyl halide is needed?
e: The acetoacetic ester synthesis makes CH₃CO–CH₂–R, where R comes from the alkyl halide.
4-Phenylbutan-2-one is CH₃CO–CH₂–CH₂C₆H₅, so R = CH₂C₆H₅, from benzyl bromide.
Bromobenzene can't do SN2, and C₆H₅CH₂CH₂Br would add one carbon too many.

q: Butane-1,3-diol is treated with excess chromic acid (Jones reagent). What is the direct oxidation product?
e: C1 is a primary alcohol: a strong oxidant takes it all the way to –COOH.
C3 is a secondary alcohol: it becomes a ketone.
CH₃–CO–CH₂–COOH = 3-oxobutanoic acid (acetoacetic acid).
t: 3-Oxobutanal is what PCC would give. Jones reagent over-oxidizes primary alcohols.
