q: The graph shows the pressure variation at one point as a sound wave passes. If the wavelength of this sound is 1.36 m, what is its speed?
e: One full cycle takes 4.0 ms on the graph, so T = 4.0 × 10⁻³ s and f = 1/T = 250 Hz.
t: On a time graph, crest-to-crest is the PERIOD, not the wavelength.

q: Chymotrypsinogen contains the full sequence of active chymotrypsin plus a few extra residues, yet it is almost inactive. What converts it to the active enzyme?
o: Cleavage of specific peptide bonds, so the chain reshapes its active site
Phosphorylation of its catalytic serine by a kinase in the pancreas
Binding of a Ca²⁺ ion that completes the Ser–His–Asp catalytic triad
Attachment of a sugar chain in the Golgi just before secretion
e: Zymogens are activated by proteolysis: in the small intestine, trypsin cuts chymotrypsinogen, and the new N-terminus forms an ion pair that reshapes the substrate pocket and oxyanion hole.
Cutting is irreversible, so the enzyme stays active until inhibited or degraded; keeping it as a zymogen until it reaches the gut protects the pancreas.

q: Many active sites use a histidine side chain as a general acid–base catalyst. Why is histidine well suited to this role?
o: Its pK<sub>a</sub> (≈ 6) lets it gain or lose H⁺ near pH 7
Its side chain is a strong acid that is always ionized
Its side chain stays positively charged at any pH
Its aromatic ring stores electrons for redox steps
e: Near physiological pH, significant amounts of both the protonated and neutral forms exist.
So histidine can donate a proton in one step and accept one in another.

q: The induced-fit model of enzyme action states that:
o: The active site changes shape as the substrate binds
The active site is rigid and fits the substrate exactly
Substrates change the enzyme's primary structure
e: Binding causes a conformational change that grips the substrate and strains it toward the transition state.
The older lock-and-key model assumed a rigid active site.

q: An enzyme speeds up a reversible reaction. Which quantity does the enzyme leave unchanged?
o: The rate constant of the forward reaction
e: An enzyme lowers E<sub>a</sub> for both directions equally, so both rate constants rise and equilibrium is reached faster.
ΔG° and K<sub>eq</sub> depend only on reactants and products, so they do not change.
t: Enzymes change how fast, never how far.

q: An allosteric enzyme with cooperative substrate binding shows what kind of rate vs. [S] curve?
e: Binding at one site makes binding at other sites easier.
This gives a sigmoidal curve, like hemoglobin's O₂-binding curve.

q: With substrate in large excess and all other conditions constant, the total enzyme concentration is doubled. What happens?
o: V<sub>max</sub> is unchanged; K<sub>m</sub> is halved
e: V<sub>max</sub> = k<sub>cat</sub>[E]<sub>T</sub>, so doubling [E]<sub>T</sub> doubles V<sub>max</sub>.
K<sub>m</sub> is a property of each enzyme molecule and its substrate, so it stays the same.

q: At 37 °C (where 2.303RT ≈ 5.9 kJ mol⁻¹), an enzyme lowers a reaction's activation energy by about 18 kJ mol⁻¹. Assuming the Arrhenius pre-factor is unchanged, by roughly what factor does the rate increase?
e: k ∝ 10<sup>−E<sub>a</sub>/(2.303RT)</sup>, so the rate ratio is 10<sup>ΔE<sub>a</sub>/(2.303RT)</sup>.
18/5.9 ≈ 3, so the rate increases by about 10³ = 1000-fold.
t: Each ~6 kJ mol⁻¹ off E<sub>a</sub> at body temperature ≈ 10× faster.

q: What distinguishes a coenzyme from a metal-ion cofactor?
o: A coenzyme is a small organic molecule, often derived from a vitamin
A coenzyme is always a protein
A coenzyme is a metal ion
A coenzyme is permanently consumed in each reaction
e: Cofactors are non-protein helpers. Inorganic ones are metal ions (for example Zn²⁺, Mg²⁺); organic ones are coenzymes (for example NAD⁺, FAD, CoA).

q: An enzyme follows Michaelis–Menten kinetics. At [S] = 3Km, what fraction of Vmax is the reaction rate?
e: v = Vmax[S] ÷ (Km + [S])
= Vmax(3Km) ÷ (Km + 3Km) = 3/4 Vmax

q: Phosphoglucomutase converts glucose-1-phosphate into glucose-6-phosphate by moving the phosphate within the same molecule. To which enzyme class does it belong?
e: The substrate and product are isomers (same formula, C₆H₁₃O₉P), so the enzyme is an isomerase. Mutases are isomerases that shift a group within one molecule.
Transferases (including kinases) move a group from one molecule to a different molecule.
t: 'Mutase' = mutate in place. If only one molecule goes in and its isomer comes out, think isomerase.

q: A competitive inhibitor has K<sub>i</sub> = 3 µM. What inhibitor concentration makes the apparent K<sub>m</sub> three times its normal value?
e: Apparent K<sub>m</sub> = K<sub>m</sub>(1 + [I]/K<sub>i</sub>). For a 3-fold increase, 1 + [I]/K<sub>i</sub> = 3.
[I] = 2K<sub>i</sub> = 2 × 3 µM = 6 µM

q: Why are enzyme kinetics measured as initial rates (v₀), using only the first few percent of the reaction?
o: [S] is near its starting value and too little product exists to react back
Enzymes are only stable for the first few seconds of an assay
K<sub>m</sub> can be defined only at the instant the reaction starts
After the first minute, every enzyme reaction becomes zero order
e: Early on, almost no substrate has been used, so [S] is known, and the reverse reaction (P → S) is negligible.
Later, falling [S], product build-up and product inhibition would all distort the rate.

q: Protein folding in water is favorable even though the folded chain is more ordered than the unfolded one. What mainly drives nonpolar side chains to the interior?
o: Ordered water around them is released, gaining entropy
Nonpolar side chains form covalent bonds in the core
Nonpolar groups hydrogen-bond strongly to each other
Burial lowers the entropy of the surrounding water
e: Water forms ordered 'cages' around exposed nonpolar groups.
Burying those groups frees the water, raising its entropy (ΔS > 0), which makes ΔG for folding negative. This is the hydrophobic effect.
t: The hydrophobic effect is about water's entropy, not attraction between oily groups.

q: A protein is treated with 8 M urea, which unfolds it without breaking covalent bonds. Which level of structure stays intact?
e: Urea disrupts hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions.
Peptide bonds (primary structure) are covalent and survive.
Disulfide bonds also survive unless a reducing agent is added.

q: Which amino acid has an imidazole ring in its side chain?
e: Histidine's imidazole ring has a pKa near 6, so it can gain or lose H⁺ near physiological pH.
That makes histidine a common acid–base catalyst in enzyme active sites.

q: The dipeptide Lys–Gly has pK<sub>a</sub> values of 3.0 (C-terminal –COOH), 8.0 (N-terminal –NH₃⁺) and 10.0 (Lys side chain). What is its isoelectric point?
e: Charges as pH rises: +2 (all protonated) → +1 after the –COOH loses H⁺ (pK<sub>a</sub> 3.0) → 0 after the N-terminus loses H⁺ (8.0) → −1 after the side chain loses H⁺ (10.0).
The neutral form lies between pK<sub>a</sub> 8.0 and 10.0: pI = (8.0 + 10.0) ÷ 2 = 9.0
t: Average the two pK<sub>a</sub> values on either side of the net-zero form, not all three.

q: A disulfide bond forms between two:
e: Two –SH groups are oxidized to form –S–S– (cystine).
Reducing agents like β-mercaptoethanol break disulfides.

q: An α-helix has 3.6 residues per turn and rises 0.54 nm per turn. About how long is a 30-residue α-helix?
e: Number of turns = 30 ÷ 3.6 ≈ 8.3 turns.
Length = 8.3 × 0.54 nm ≈ 4.5 nm (equivalently 0.15 nm per residue × 30).

q: In a neurodegenerative disease, a normal brain protein and its disease form have the identical amino acid sequence. The disease form resists proteases, is insoluble, and forms stacked fibrils held by H-bonds between backbone strands. What best describes the change?
o: α-Helical regions refolded into stacked β-sheets
A point mutation changed the protein's sequence
Peptide bonds were replaced with disulfide bonds
β-Sheets unfolded into a soluble random coil
e: Same sequence means primary structure is unchanged; the difference is in folding (secondary/tertiary structure).
Backbone H-bonds between stacked strands describe β-sheets; these amyloid fibrils are insoluble and protease-resistant, as in prion diseases.

q: Lowering the pH of a folded protein's solution from 7 to 2 often unfolds it. Which effect contributes most directly?
o: Carboxylates gain H⁺, breaking salt bridges
Peptide bonds break, destroying the primary structure
H⁺ ions reduce the protein's disulfide bonds
Amino groups lose H⁺, adding negative charge
e: At pH 2, Asp and Glu side chains become neutral –COOH.
Their salt bridges with Lys/Arg are lost, and the protein carries many repelling + charges, so it unfolds.
Peptide bonds stay intact; primary structure is unchanged.

q: A researcher unfolds an enzyme with urea and β-mercaptoethanol, then slowly removes both. The enzyme refolds and becomes fully active again. What does this show?
o: The primary sequence contains all the information needed for folding
Chaperones must be present for the protein to refold correctly
Disulfide bonds, not the sequence, dictate the folded structure
Urea and β-mercaptoethanol never fully denatured the enzyme
e: Removing the denaturants let the chain refold on its own into its active shape.
So the primary sequence alone determines the 3D structure (Anfinsen's classic experiment).
t: Real cells use chaperones to prevent misfolding and aggregation, but the folding information is in the sequence.

q: In a β-pleated sheet, where do the side chains of consecutive residues along one strand point?
o: Alternately above and below the plane of the sheet
All toward the neighboring strand to form H-bonds
All outward from a central axis, as in a helix
All into the sheet's plane, between the strands
e: The backbone N–H and C=O groups make the H-bonds between strands, within the plane.
Side chains alternate up and down, so one face of a sheet can be nonpolar and the other polar.
t: Helix: side chains point out like bristles; sheet: they alternate up and down.

q: Which amino acid has a guanidinium group (a carbon bonded to three nitrogens) at the end of its side chain?
e: Arginine's side chain ends in –NH–C(=NH₂⁺)–NH₂, a guanidinium group.
Lysine ends in a simple –NH₃⁺, histidine has an imidazole ring and asparagine has an amide.
t: Arg has the 'arg-uably' most basic side chain (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 12.5): it stays positive at almost any pH in the body.

q: Which standard amino acid is achiral?
e: A chiral α-carbon needs four different groups.
Glycine's side chain is just H, so its α-carbon has two identical H atoms.
w: Alanine has a CH₃ side chain.
Serine has a CH₂OH side chain.
Cysteine has a CH₂SH side chain.

q: A restriction enzyme recognizes a specific 6-base-pair sequence. In random DNA with equal amounts of each base, about how often would its site occur?
e: Each position matches with probability 1/4.
(1/4)⁶ = 1/4096, so on average one site per 4⁶ = 4096 bp.
t: 4-cutter: 4⁴ = 256 bp; 6-cutter: 4⁶ ≈ 4 kb; 8-cutter: 4⁸ ≈ 65 kb.

q: A 6.0 kb circular plasmid has one EcoRI site and one BamHI site, 1.5 kb apart. What fragments appear on a gel after cutting with both enzymes?
e: Two cuts in a circle give two linear pieces.
One piece is the 1.5 kb between the sites; the other is the rest: 6.0 − 1.5 = 4.5 kb.
t: n cuts in a circular plasmid give n fragments; n cuts in a linear DNA give n + 1.

q: Chromatin is briefly treated with a nuclease that can cut only exposed DNA. The DNA fragments come out in sizes of about 200, 400 and 600 bp. What best explains this pattern?
o: Histones protect wrapped DNA, so cuts fall in the linker DNA between them
The nuclease recognizes one specific sequence that repeats every 200 bp
Each gene in the genome is exactly 200 bp long
Histones themselves cut DNA into 200 bp pieces during replication
e: About 147 bp of DNA wraps each histone octamer (two each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4), and short linker DNA joins neighboring nucleosomes.
Only linker DNA is exposed, so partial digestion gives one-nucleosome units (~200 bp) and their multiples: the 'nucleosome ladder'.
t: Beads on a string: the beads (nucleosomes) are protected; the string (linker) gets cut.

q: Why does every base pair in a DNA double helix contain one purine and one pyrimidine?
o: It keeps the helix width constant along its length
It lets each pair form exactly 3 hydrogen bonds
It makes the two strands run in the same direction
It puts all the bases on the outside of the helix
e: A purine (two rings) + pyrimidine (one ring) always spans about the same distance (~2 nm).
Two purines would bulge the helix and two pyrimidines would pinch it; A–T pairs have only 2 H-bonds.

q: In agarose gel electrophoresis of DNA, which fragments travel farthest?
e: All DNA is negatively charged and moves toward the + electrode.
Smaller fragments slip through the gel's pores faster.

q: An RT-PCR assay measures a gene's mRNA in tissue. Why are the primers often placed in two different exons, flanking an intron?
o: So genomic DNA gives a longer or no product
So reverse transcriptase can splice the RNA
So the primers bind both mRNA strands
So the product lacks the 5′ cap and tail
e: cDNA from spliced mRNA lacks the intron, giving a short product.
Contaminating genomic DNA still has the intron, so it gives a much longer product (or none), which can be told apart.

q: Telomerase helps maintain chromosome ends by:
o: Adding repeated DNA sequences to the 3′ ends, using its own RNA template
Adding repeated DNA sequences to the 5′ ends, using a DNA template
Joining Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand at chromosome ends
Trimming excess repeats from the 3′ overhang after each replication
e: Telomerase is a reverse transcriptase that carries its own RNA template.
It's active in stem cells and many cancer cells.
w: It uses its own RNA template.

q: Which bases are purines?
e: Purines have two fused rings: adenine and guanine ('Pure As Gold').
Pyrimidines have one ring: cytosine, thymine and uracil.

q: A cloning plasmid carries a gene for ampicillin resistance. After a transformation, the bacteria are spread on plates containing ampicillin. Why?
o: Only cells that took up the plasmid can grow
Ampicillin makes the bacteria take up more plasmid
Ampicillin cuts the plasmid so the insert can enter
Only cells without the plasmid can grow
e: Transformation is inefficient; most cells take up no plasmid.
The resistance gene lets plasmid-carrying cells survive on ampicillin, so every colony that grows contains the plasmid.

q: Gene therapy using a retroviral vector differs from an adenoviral vector mainly because the retroviral vector:
o: Integrates its DNA into the host genome
Stays as a separate episome in the nucleus
Delivers RNA that is never copied into DNA
Can enter only cells that lack a nucleus
e: Retroviruses reverse-transcribe their RNA into DNA, which integrates into a host chromosome.
This gives lasting expression but risks insertional mutagenesis; adenoviral DNA stays episomal and is lost as cells divide.

q: As helicase unwinds DNA at a replication fork, which enzyme relieves the overwinding (supercoiling) that builds up ahead of the fork?
e: Unwinding the strands twists the DNA ahead of the fork more tightly.
Topoisomerases cut and rejoin DNA strands to release that tension.

q: Which enzyme makes the short RNA primers that DNA polymerase extends during replication?
e: DNA polymerase cannot start a chain from scratch; it needs a free 3′-OH.
Primase lays down short RNA primers that supply that 3′-OH.

q: In bacteria, the Shine–Dalgarno sequence on an mRNA:
o: Pairs with 16S rRNA to place the ribosome at the start codon
Pairs with the anticodon of the initiator tRNA
Signals RNA polymerase to stop transcription
Is removed by splicing before translation begins
e: The Shine–Dalgarno sequence lies a few bases upstream of AUG.
It base-pairs with the 3′ end of 16S rRNA in the small subunit, lining up the start codon in the P site.

q: Rifampin binds bacterial RNA polymerase and blocks new RNA synthesis, yet it does not bind ribosomes. Why does bacterial protein synthesis fall within minutes of treatment?
o: Bacterial mRNAs have short lifetimes, so the existing supply is quickly used up
Rifampin is converted into tetracycline inside the bacterial cell
Bacterial ribosomes are made of protein that rifampin degrades
Bacteria translate only DNA directly, not RNA
e: Most bacterial mRNAs last only a few minutes before being degraded.
With transcription blocked, no new mRNA replaces them, so translation quickly stops for lack of templates.

q: α-Amanitin, a toxin from death cap mushrooms, strongly inhibits RNA polymerase II. In poisoned liver cells, what is the most immediate effect?
o: New mRNA synthesis stops, while rRNA synthesis continues
New rRNA synthesis stops, while mRNA synthesis continues
DNA replication stops, while all transcription continues
Translation stops at once, while transcription continues
e: RNA polymerase II makes the pre-mRNAs for protein-coding genes; Pol I (rRNA) is resistant to α-amanitin.
Without new mRNA, protein synthesis fades as existing mRNAs decay, and liver cells die.
t: α-Amanitin targets Pol II — the mRNA maker — which is why death cap poisoning destroys the liver.

q: In E. coli, the trp operon is shut off when tryptophan is abundant. Tryptophan acts as a:
o: Corepressor that helps the repressor bind the operator
Substrate for the repressor's enzyme activity
e: The trp operon is repressible: tryptophan binds the repressor and activates it.
The active repressor binds the operator and blocks transcription.
By contrast, the lac operon is inducible: lactose (allolactose) inactivates its repressor.

q: How many codons specify amino acids in the standard genetic code?
e: 4 bases taken 3 at a time: 4³ = 64 codons.
3 are stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA).
64 − 3 = 61 code for amino acids. The code is 'degenerate': most amino acids have more than one codon.
t: Degeneracy is why many point mutations in the third codon position are silent.
w: 20 is the number of amino acids.

q: The 5′ cap of a eukaryotic mRNA is:
o: A string of adenines added after cleavage
A ribosome-binding sequence encoded in DNA
e: The cap is added soon after transcription starts: a methylated G is linked through its 5′ carbon to the mRNA's 5′ end by a triphosphate bridge.
The poly-A tail, not the cap, is the string of adenines at the 3′ end.

q: Introns are removed from pre-mRNA by the:
e: The spliceosome, made of snRNAs and proteins, cuts out introns and joins exons.

q: Which base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
e: RNA uses uracil in place of thymine; uracil pairs with adenine.

q: An E. coli strain has a lacI mutation that makes a nonfunctional repressor. When grown with no lactose and no glucose, its lac genes are:
o: Transcribed at a high level anyway
Silent, because no inducer is present
Transcribed only after lactose is added
e: With no working repressor, nothing blocks the operator, so expression no longer requires lactose (constitutive).
With glucose absent, cAMP–CAP is bound, so transcription is high.
t: Broken repressor (lacI⁻) = always on. CAP still needs low glucose for high-level transcription.

q: Which codon starts translation?
e: AUG codes for methionine and marks the start.
UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons.

q: In bacteria, ribosomes can begin translating an mRNA before its transcription is finished, but this does not happen in human cells. Why?
o: Human transcription occurs in the nucleus, and translation in the cytoplasm
Human ribosomes can bind only the 3′ end of an mRNA
Bacterial mRNAs are made 3′→5′, so the start codon leaves the polymerase last
Human mRNAs have no start codon until they are spliced
e: Bacteria have no nucleus, so a new mRNA's 5′ end is exposed to ribosomes while RNA polymerase is still working.
In eukaryotes, pre-mRNA is capped, spliced and exported from the nucleus before ribosomes can reach it.

q: During translation, an mRNA codon pairs with a complementary:
e: Each tRNA carries an amino acid and a 3-base anticodon that matches a codon on the mRNA.

q: An infant is weaned onto fruit juice and develops vomiting and low blood glucose after each feeding. The liver lacks aldolase B. Fructose-1-phosphate builds up in hepatocytes. What best explains the hypoglycemia?
o: Fructose-1-phosphate traps phosphate, so ATP and Pi fall and glycogen breakdown stalls
Fructose is converted to glucose too quickly, so insulin overshoots and stays high
Fructose-1-phosphate activates glucose-6-phosphatase, so glucose is lost in urine
The missing aldolase B is needed for every step of glycolysis in the liver cell's cytosol
e: Fructokinase keeps phosphorylating fructose, but without aldolase B the fructose-1-phosphate can't be split, so phosphate is tied up.
Low Pi starves glycogen phosphorylase (which uses Pi) and lowers ATP, so the liver can't release glucose; gluconeogenesis also suffers.
Treatment is removing fructose and sucrose from the diet.

q: What are the two main products of the pentose phosphate pathway?
e: The oxidative phase makes NADPH (for fatty acid synthesis and antioxidant defense).
The non-oxidative phase makes ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotides.

q: A malnourished person who has not eaten for two days drinks heavily and becomes hypoglycemic. Ethanol oxidation in the liver produces large amounts of NADH. Why does this cause hypoglycemia?
o: High NADH pushes pyruvate to lactate and OAA to malate, starving gluconeogenesis
High NADH activates glycogen synthase, locking glucose away in liver glycogen
Ethanol is converted into insulin precursors, raising insulin secretion
NADH allosterically inhibits glucose-6-phosphatase inside the liver ER lumen
e: After two days without food, liver glycogen is gone, so blood glucose depends on gluconeogenesis.
Alcohol and acetaldehyde dehydrogenases raise NADH:NAD⁺, shifting lactate dehydrogenase and malate dehydrogenase toward lactate and malate.
Pyruvate and oxaloacetate, the starting materials of gluconeogenesis, become scarce, so glucose output falls.
t: Fasting + alcohol = high hypoglycemia risk: no glycogen and a choked gluconeogenesis.

q: During a long fast, which organ is the main site of gluconeogenesis?
e: Gluconeogenesis builds new glucose from lactate, glycerol and amino acids.
The liver does most of it (the kidney cortex helps during long fasts).
Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so it cannot release free glucose into blood.
t: Liver = the body's glucose bank for everyone else. Muscle keeps glucose for itself.
w: The brain uses glucose; it doesn't make much.

q: Which glycolytic enzyme is also used in gluconeogenesis, simply running in reverse?
e: Seven glycolytic steps are near equilibrium and run in either direction, including enolase.
Hexokinase, PFK-1 and pyruvate kinase are irreversible in cells and are bypassed by four gluconeogenic enzymes: pyruvate carboxylase, PEPCK, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase.
t: 3 irreversible glycolytic steps, 4 bypass enzymes.

q: In liver, glucagon triggers protein kinase A to phosphorylate the bifunctional enzyme PFK-2/FBPase-2. What follows?
o: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate falls, slowing glycolysis and favoring gluconeogenesis
Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate rises, speeding glycolysis and slowing gluconeogenesis
PFK-1 itself is phosphorylated and becomes fully active in the liver cell
Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate falls, which speeds glycolysis in the liver
e: Phosphorylation inactivates the kinase domain (PFK-2) and activates the phosphatase domain (FBPase-2).
Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is broken down, removing the strongest activator of PFK-1 and the inhibition of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase.
Net: liver glycolysis slows and gluconeogenesis speeds up.

q: In liver, pyruvate kinase is activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, the product of the PFK-1 step. This is an example of:
o: Feed-forward activation by an earlier intermediate
Feedback inhibition by the pathway's end product
Covalent regulation by protein kinase A phosphorylation
Competitive activation at the enzyme's active site
e: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is made upstream (by PFK-1) and activates a later enzyme, pyruvate kinase.
When PFK-1 speeds up, pyruvate kinase gets ready to handle the coming flow of intermediates, so they don't pile up.

q: Which enzyme is unique to gluconeogenesis (not used in glycolysis)?
e: Gluconeogenesis bypasses glycolysis's 3 irreversible steps using: pyruvate carboxylase and PEPCK, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, and glucose-6-phosphatase.

q: Skeletal muscle and adipose tissue lack fructokinase. How does dietary fructose that reaches these tissues enter glycolysis?
o: Aldolase B splits it directly into two trioses
Fructokinase in the blood phosphorylates it first
It must first be converted to glucose by the liver
e: Hexokinase has broad specificity and can phosphorylate fructose at C6, though with much lower affinity than for glucose.
Fructose-6-phosphate is already a glycolytic intermediate, so it continues at the PFK-1 step. (In liver, fructokinase makes fructose-1-phosphate instead.)

q: What does glycolysis produce from one glucose molecule?
e: Glucose (6C) splits into two 3-carbon pyruvates.
Net yield: 2 ATP and 2 NADH.

q: What is the net ATP produced by glycolysis per molecule of glucose?
e: Investment phase uses 2 ATP.
Payoff phase makes 4 ATP (plus 2 NADH).
Net = 4 − 2 = 2 ATP
t: Glycolysis happens in the cytosol and needs no O₂.
w: 36 is an older total for complete oxidation.

q: In the Cori cycle, lactate from exercising muscle is:
o: Carried to the liver and converted back to glucose
Burned directly by the muscle for ATP
Converted into fatty acids in muscle
e: Muscle makes lactate during intense exercise.
The liver uses it for gluconeogenesis and sends glucose back to the muscle.
w: Muscle sends lactate to the liver.
Muscle doesn't make fat from it.

q: Oxidizing one acetyl-CoA in the citric acid cycle yields 3 NADH and 1 FADH₂. Passing all these electrons to oxygen consumes how many O₂ molecules?
e: Each NADH or FADH₂ carries 2 electrons: 4 carriers × 2 = 8 e⁻.
O₂ + 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻ → 2 H₂O, so 8 e⁻ ÷ 4 = 2 O₂.

q: Which mobile carrier moves electrons from Complex III to Complex IV?
e: Cytochrome c is a small water-soluble heme protein on the intermembrane-space side of the inner membrane.
It carries one electron at a time (Fe³⁺ ⇌ Fe²⁺) from Complex III to Complex IV.
t: Order of carriers: NADH → I → Q → III → cyt c → IV → O₂.

q: How many CO₂ molecules are released when one glucose is fully oxidized through pyruvate dehydrogenase and the citric acid cycle?
e: PDH: 1 CO₂ per pyruvate × 2 = 2.
Citric acid cycle: 2 CO₂ per acetyl-CoA × 2 = 4.
Total = 6, accounting for all 6 carbons of glucose.
w: That counts only the PDH step.

q: Which pair of signals activates isocitrate dehydrogenase?
e: ADP signals that the cell needs energy; Ca²⁺ signals muscle contraction.
ATP and NADH, signs of plenty, inhibit the enzyme, slowing the cycle when energy is high.

q: When citric acid cycle intermediates are drawn off for biosynthesis, which reaction most directly refills oxaloacetate?
o: Citrate lyase: citrate → acetyl-CoA + OAA in cytosol
e: Reactions that replenish cycle intermediates are called anaplerotic.
Pyruvate carboxylase adds CO₂ to pyruvate in the matrix, making new oxaloacetate.
Acetyl-CoA only cycles through; it can't add net carbon to the pool.
t: Anaplerotic = 'filling up.' Acetyl-CoA keeps the cycle turning but never refills it.

q: Mitochondria swollen in a hypotonic buffer rupture their outer membrane. They then oxidize succinate very slowly, and adding purified cytochrome c restores the normal rate. What explains this?
o: Cytochrome c, a soluble carrier in the intermembrane space, was lost
Succinate dehydrogenase leaked out of the damaged outer membrane
Cytochrome c is needed to carry succinate into the matrix
Rupture let cytochrome c enter the matrix, where it blocks Complex II
e: Cytochrome c is a small water-soluble protein loosely attached to the outer face of the inner membrane.
When the outer membrane breaks, cytochrome c washes out, and electrons can't get from Complex III to Complex IV until it is added back.

q: Rotenone blocks Complex I. In a cell exposed to rotenone, which fuel can still feed electrons into the ETC?
e: Complex II passes electrons directly to coenzyme Q, bypassing Complex I.
So succinate oxidation can still drive some proton pumping (through Complexes III and IV) and ATP synthesis.

q: Isolated mitochondria are given succinate and Pi, and O₂ use is slow. Adding ADP makes O₂ use jump; it slows again once the ADP has been converted to ATP. What does this show?
o: Electron transport is tightly coupled to ATP synthesis
ADP is the final electron acceptor of the chain
Succinate can't be oxidized until ADP activates Complex II
ADP uncouples mitochondria and lets protons leak in
e: Without ADP, ATP synthase is idle, the proton gradient grows, and pumping (and thus electron flow) is opposed.
ADP lets H⁺ flow through ATP synthase, lowering the gradient, so electrons and O₂ use speed up.
This 'respiratory control' means mitochondria burn fuel only as fast as ATP is needed.

q: Which vitamin–coenzyme pairing is correct?
e: Pantothenic acid is part of coenzyme A.
Riboflavin forms FAD and FMN; niacin forms NAD⁺ and NADP⁺; thiamine forms thiamine pyrophosphate. Lipoic acid is not a B vitamin derivative.
t: B₁ thiamine → TPP, B₂ riboflavin → FAD, B₃ niacin → NAD⁺, B₅ pantothenate → CoA, B₆ → PLP.

q: In mitochondrial ATP synthase, where is ATP actually made?
o: In the F₁ head, which faces the matrix
In the F₀ ring, within the inner membrane
In the F₁ head, which faces the intermembrane space
In cytochrome c oxidase, next to the synthase
e: F₀ is the membrane-embedded proton channel; H⁺ flow through it spins a rotor.
The rotor turns inside F₁, which projects into the matrix, where conformational changes make ATP from ADP + Pi.

q: Where is ATP synthase located?
e: ATP synthase spans the inner membrane, with its catalytic head facing the matrix.

q: A child with pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency has lactic acidosis that worsens after carbohydrate-rich meals. Which diet best supplies acetyl-CoA to the brain without needing PDH?
o: A high-carbohydrate diet with frequent small meals
A high-protein diet rich in alanine
A diet high in sucrose and fructose
e: Carbohydrate makes pyruvate, which can't enter the citric acid cycle without PDH, so it becomes lactate.
Fat makes ketone bodies, which the brain converts to acetyl-CoA directly, bypassing PDH. Alanine and fructose both feed into pyruvate, which doesn't help.

q: Where in the cell does β-oxidation of fatty acids occur?
e: Fatty acids are activated (fatty acyl-CoA) in the cytosol.
The carnitine shuttle moves them into the mitochondria.
β-Oxidation happens in the mitochondrial matrix, making acetyl-CoA, NADH and FADH₂.
t: Fatty acid synthesis is in the cytosol; breakdown is in the mitochondria. Opposite places for opposite jobs.
w: Activation is in the cytosol. Oxidation isn't.

q: Liver cells making fatty acids are given H¹⁴CO₃⁻. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase uses this bicarbonate to make malonyl-CoA. Where does the ¹⁴C end up?
o: Nowhere in palmitate: the added CO₂ is released at each condensation
In every second carbon of palmitate, starting from the carboxyl end
Only in the carboxyl carbon (C1) of the finished palmitate chain
In the methyl end of palmitate, carried in by the acetyl-CoA primer
e: Each malonyl group gives up the CO₂ that acetyl-CoA carboxylase added when it condenses with the growing chain.
The decarboxylation drives the condensation forward, and the labeled carbon leaves as CO₂, so none ends up in palmitate.
t: The CO₂ put on by acetyl-CoA carboxylase is a 'loaner': decarboxylation pays for each C–C bond.

q: Besides the pentose phosphate pathway, which reaction supplies NADPH for fatty acid synthesis?
e: When citrate is exported and cleaved in the cytosol, its oxaloacetate is reduced to malate.
Malic enzyme oxidatively decarboxylates malate to pyruvate, reducing NADP⁺ to NADPH.
Malate and lactate dehydrogenases use NAD⁺/NADH, not NADPH.

q: Hormone-sensitive lipase breaks down stored fat. Which hormone inhibits it?
e: Glucagon and epinephrine activate it (through cAMP and PKA) during fasting and stress.
Insulin inhibits it in the fed state, so fat is stored.

q: Which urea cycle reaction takes place in the mitochondrial matrix?
e: Carbamoyl phosphate formation and the ornithine transcarbamylase step happen in the matrix.
Citrulline is exported; argininosuccinate synthetase, argininosuccinate lyase and arginase work in the cytosol.
Ornithine then re-enters the mitochondrion.

q: Which lipoprotein carries dietary triglycerides from the intestine to tissues?
e: Chylomicrons: dietary fat from the intestine. VLDL: fat made by the liver. LDL: cholesterol delivery. HDL: cholesterol return to the liver.

q: The liver makes ketone bodies but can't use them for energy. Why?
o: The liver lacks thiophorase, which converts acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA
Ketone bodies can't cross liver cell membranes to reach the mitochondria
The liver lacks HMG-CoA synthase, which is needed to oxidize ketone bodies
Ketone bodies inhibit β-oxidation, so the liver avoids burning them
e: Using ketones requires succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase.
The liver lacks it, so it exports ketones for other tissues to use.

q: Statins lower cholesterol by inhibiting:
e: HMG-CoA reductase catalyzes the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis.
w: That frees fatty acids from lipoproteins.

q: About how much net ATP does complete oxidation of palmitate yield? (2.5 ATP per NADH, 1.5 per FADH₂, 10 per acetyl-CoA; activation costs 2 ATP equivalents)
e: 7 rounds: 7 NADH (17.5) + 7 FADH₂ (10.5) = 28 ATP.
8 acetyl-CoA × 10 = 80 ATP.
108 − 2 for activation = 106 ATP
t: Older textbooks (3 and 2 ATP per NADH and FADH₂) give 129. Use whatever ratio the question gives you.
w: Recheck the NADH and FADH₂ totals.
This forgets the 2 ATP for activation.

q: The two nitrogen atoms in each urea molecule come directly from:
o: Two molecules of glutamine side-chain N
Ornithine and citrulline, the cycle's carriers
e: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I uses free NH₄⁺ to make carbamoyl phosphate, which carries the first N.
Aspartate adds the second N when it joins citrulline to form argininosuccinate.
Ornithine is a carrier that is regenerated each turn.

q: How many high-energy phosphate bonds are used to make one urea molecule?
o: 4, since one of the 3 ATP is split to AMP + PPi
3, since each of the 3 ATP is split to ADP
2, since only carbamoyl phosphate needs ATP
6, since each nitrogen costs 3 ATP to fix
e: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I uses 2 ATP → 2 ADP (2 bonds).
Argininosuccinate synthetase uses 1 ATP → AMP + PPi, and PPi hydrolysis spends a second bond: 2 + 2 = 4.
t: ATP → AMP + PPi counts as 2 ATP equivalents, because PPi hydrolysis spends a second bond.

q: A patient with a carcinoid tumor makes huge amounts of serotonin and develops signs of niacin deficiency (pellagra). What is the best explanation?
o: Tryptophan, the precursor of both, is diverted to serotonin
Tyrosine, the precursor of both, is diverted to serotonin
Serotonin directly blocks niacin absorption in the gut
Histidine, the precursor of both, is used up making serotonin
e: Serotonin (and melatonin) are made from tryptophan.
The body can also make some niacin (for NAD⁺) from tryptophan.
When the tumor uses most of the tryptophan, niacin synthesis falls and pellagra can appear.

q: A child has very high blood LDL cholesterol and cholesterol deposits in the skin. Cultured cells from the child cannot internalize labeled LDL. Which defect is most likely?
o: Defective clathrin in red blood cells
e: Cells take in LDL by receptor-mediated endocytosis.
Without functional LDL receptors (familial hypercholesterolemia), LDL can't be cleared from the blood, and cells sense too little cholesterol, so they keep making more.

q: In cystic fibrosis, a defective CFTR protein causes thick, sticky mucus in the lungs. CFTR is a:
e: CFTR lets Cl⁻ exit epithelial cells, and water follows by osmosis.
Without it, secretions are dehydrated and thick.

q: Digoxin inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase in heart muscle. Why does this strengthen contractions?
o: A weaker Na⁺ gradient slows Ca²⁺ removal by the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger, raising Ca²⁺
More K⁺ accumulates inside the cell, which makes each action potential stronger
It blocks L-type Ca²⁺ channels, so more Ca²⁺ is retained inside the cell
Sparing the ATP used by the pump leaves more ATP for myosin cross-bridges
e: Blocking the pump raises intracellular Na⁺.
The Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger then has a weaker gradient to work with, so Ca²⁺ builds up inside.
More Ca²⁺ means stronger contractions.

q: Why is the equilibrium potential for Na⁺ positive (about +60 mV)?
o: Na⁺ is much more concentrated outside the cell
Na⁺ is more concentrated inside the cell
e: Na⁺ flows inward down its gradient until the inside becomes positive enough to stop it.
That balancing voltage is positive inside.

q: Which pair is correctly ordered from MORE permeable to LESS permeable across a pure lipid bilayer?
e: Small, nonpolar or weakly polar molecules cross fastest; large polar molecules and ions cross slowest.
Small ethanol crosses easily; glucose is large and polar. Water, urea and CO₂ all cross better than glucose or ions.

q: Lipid rafts are small, more ordered membrane patches that cluster certain signaling proteins. They are enriched in:
e: Sphingolipids have long, mostly saturated chains that pack tightly with cholesterol.
This forms thicker, less fluid domains that float within the surrounding bilayer.

q: A hydropathy plot of a newly sequenced membrane protein shows seven separate stretches of about 20 hydrophobic amino acids. What is the most likely structure?
o: Seven transmembrane α-helices, as in a G protein-coupled receptor
One transmembrane helix, as in a receptor tyrosine kinase
A peripheral protein bound only to the membrane's surface
A soluble cytosolic protein with seven buried strands
e: Each hydrophobic stretch of about 20 residues is long enough to form one membrane-spanning α-helix.
Seven such segments suggest a seven-pass protein, the signature of GPCRs.
t: GPCRs are often called 7TM (seven-transmembrane) or serpentine receptors.

q: GLUT1 behaves like an enzyme with K<sub>m</sub> ≈ 1 mM for glucose. At a blood glucose of 4 mM, about what fraction of its maximum rate is it working?
e: Rate/V<sub>max</sub> = [S]/(K<sub>m</sub> + [S]).
= 4/(1 + 4) = 0.80, so about 80% of V<sub>max</sub>.

q: Aspirin (a weak acid, pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 3.5) crosses cell membranes mainly in its neutral form. In an overdose, giving IV bicarbonate to raise urine pH to about 8 speeds its excretion. Why?
o: In basic urine it is mostly ionized, so it can't diffuse back across the tubule cells
In basic urine it is mostly neutral, so it dissolves better in the urine
Bicarbonate breaks aspirin into smaller pieces that the glomerulus filters faster
Basic urine opens membrane channels that secrete the neutral drug
e: For a weak acid, pH above pK<sub>a</sub> favors the deprotonated (charged) form; at pH 8 (about 4.5 units above pK<sub>a</sub>) almost all of it is ionized.
Charged molecules cross the tubule cell membranes poorly, so the drug is trapped in the urine and excreted instead of reabsorbed (ion trapping).
t: Weak acid in base, or weak base in acid → charged → trapped on that side of the membrane.

q: SGLT1 moves glucose into intestinal cells together with Na⁺, against glucose's concentration gradient. This is:
e: SGLT1 uses no ATP directly.
It uses the Na⁺ gradient made by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (which DOES use ATP). That makes it secondary active transport.

q: Tumor cells that survived chemotherapy resist several unrelated drugs and keep less of a fluorescent dye inside. Depleting the cells' ATP restores dye buildup. Which explanation fits best?
o: An ATP-driven pump such as P-glycoprotein exports the drugs
The cells' membranes became impermeable to every kind of solute
A passive channel lets the drugs leak out of the cells
The drugs are broken down by ATP-requiring enzymes
e: Low dye and drug levels that recover when ATP is removed point to active efflux.
P-glycoprotein, an ABC transporter, uses ATP to pump many hydrophobic drugs out, giving multidrug resistance.

q: Most integral membrane proteins can be removed from a membrane only with detergents. Why?
o: Their nonpolar surfaces interact with the fatty acid tails of the bilayer
They are covalently bonded to the phosphate head groups of the membrane lipids
They are held by ionic bonds to the extracellular matrix
They are too large to fit through the membrane's pores
e: Integral proteins have hydrophobic regions buried among the lipid tails.
Only an amphipathic detergent can replace the lipids around those regions and carry the protein into solution.

q: In size-exclusion (gel-filtration) chromatography, which proteins come off the column first?
e: Small proteins enter the beads' pores and take a longer path.
Large proteins are excluded from the pores and flow straight through, eluting first.
w: Small proteins enter the pores and come out last.

q: A mixture of protein P (pI 4.5) and protein Q (pI 10.0) is loaded onto a cation-exchange column (negatively charged beads) at pH 7.0. What happens?
o: P flows through; Q binds until eluted with salt
Q flows through; P binds until eluted with salt
Both bind, because both are charged at pH 7
Neither binds, because the beads are neutral at pH 7
e: At pH 7, P (pI 4.5) is above its pI, so it is negative and is repelled by the negative beads.
Q (pI 10) is below its pI, so it is positive and binds; raising salt later releases it.

q: Adding a high concentration of ammonium sulfate makes proteins precipitate (salting out). What is the main reason?
o: Salt ions bind water, leaving too little to hydrate proteins
Sulfate ions cleave the protein's peptide bonds
Ammonium ions reduce the protein's disulfide bonds
Salt raises the protein's net charge and solubility
e: At high salt, water molecules are tied up hydrating the many small ions.
Proteins lose their hydration shells, and their exposed nonpolar patches stick together. The precipitate can usually be redissolved still active.

q: In a rare hemoglobin variant, positively charged residues lining the central cavity, where 2,3-BPG binds deoxyhemoglobin, are replaced with neutral ones. People with this variant have unusually high red blood cell counts. What best explains this?
o: Weaker BPG binding raises O₂ affinity, so tissues get less O₂ and more EPO is made
Stronger BPG binding lowers O₂ affinity, flooding the tissues with O₂
The variant loses all cooperativity and cannot bind O₂ in the lungs
The variant cannot carry CO₂, so the blood becomes acidic
e: Negatively charged 2,3-BPG binds the positive residues in the cavity and stabilizes the T state; removing those charges weakens BPG binding.
With less BPG bound, Hb stays in the high-affinity form and releases less O₂ to tissues. The kidney senses low tissue O₂ and makes more erythropoietin (EPO), raising the RBC count.

q: Chymotrypsin cleaves peptide bonds on the carboxyl side of Phe, Tyr and Trp. Which fragments form when it digests Gly–Phe–Ala–Trp–Lys?
e: Cut after Phe (position 2) and after Trp (position 4).
Fragments: Gly–Phe | Ala–Trp | Lys.
t: Chymotrypsin likes big aromatics; trypsin likes the positive Lys/Arg.

q: Proteins marked for destruction by the proteasome are usually first tagged with chains of which small protein?
e: Enzymes attach chains of ubiquitin to lysine side chains of the target.
The 26S proteasome recognizes polyubiquitin, unfolds the protein, and cuts it into short peptides.

q: Which motor protein usually carries cargo along microtubules toward the plus end (toward the cell periphery)?
e: Kinesin walks toward the + end (outward).
Dynein walks toward the − end (inward). Myosin moves along actin, not microtubules.
w: Dynein walks toward the minus end.
Actin is a track, not a motor.

q: Two different proteins run as a single band at 55 kDa on SDS-PAGE. On a two-dimensional gel (isoelectric focusing first, then SDS-PAGE), they appear as two separate spots. What does this show?
o: They have similar masses but different isoelectric points
They have similar pI values but different masses
They form a 110 kDa dimer that 2D gels break apart
IEF digests one protein into a smaller fragment
e: SDS-PAGE alone separates by mass only, so similar masses overlap.
The first dimension (IEF) separates by pI, so proteins with different pI values move to different horizontal positions.

q: Many proteins are least soluble in water at a pH equal to their isoelectric point. Why?
o: With no net charge, molecules don't repel and they aggregate
Peptide bonds hydrolyze fastest at the isoelectric point
All side chains are fully protonated at the pI
The protein carries its largest net charge at the pI
e: At the pI, positive and negative charges balance (net 0).
Without like-charge repulsion between molecules, they clump together and precipitate.

q: On a Western blot, an antibody to protein K detects two closely spaced bands near 60 kDa in growth-factor-stimulated cells, but only the lower band in unstimulated cells. Treating the stimulated lysate with a phosphatase before electrophoresis leaves only the lower band. What is the best conclusion?
o: Stimulation phosphorylates K, slowing its migration
Stimulation cleaves K into a smaller active fragment
The upper band is an unrelated protein the antibody binds
Stimulation joins two K molecules by a disulfide bond
e: A phosphatase removes phosphate groups; it made the upper band disappear, so the upper band is phosphorylated K.
Added phosphates (and charge) slow the protein slightly in the gel, creating the shift. Cleavage would give a lower band, and a dimer would run near 120 kDa.

q: Cells are treated with a Gs-coupled receptor agonist that raises cAMP. A second drug then activates a Gi-coupled receptor on the same cells. What happens?
o: cAMP falls because Gαi inhibits adenylyl cyclase
cAMP rises further because Gαi also activates PKA
Ca²⁺ rises because Gαi stimulates phospholipase C
Nothing changes, because Gi needs a receptor tyrosine kinase
e: Gαs stimulates adenylyl cyclase; Gαi inhibits it.
With both active, cyclase activity drops, so cAMP and PKA activity decrease.

q: An antibody's antigen-binding site is formed by:
o: The variable regions of the heavy and light chains
The constant regions of the heavy chains
e: The tips of the antibody's Y have variable sequences that make each antibody specific.
The Fc (constant) region interacts with immune cells and complement.

q: Glucose is classified as an:
e: Glucose has 6 carbons (hexose) and an aldehyde at C1 (aldo-).
w: Glucose has 6 carbons and an aldehyde.

q: A patient feels bloating and gas after drinking milk. Which explanation fits best?
o: Low lactase lets undigested lactose reach colon bacteria, which ferment it
Excess lactase breaks lactose down too fast, flooding the gut with glucose
Milk proteins inhibit pancreatic amylase, so undigested starch reaches the colon
Low sucrase lets undigested sucrose reach the colon, where it is fermented
e: Without enough lactase, lactose can't be split into absorbable monosaccharides.
Colon bacteria ferment it, producing gas and drawing water into the gut (osmotic diarrhea).

q: Hyaluronic acid, a long glycosaminoglycan in joint fluid and cartilage, is built from repeating disaccharides that each contain a carboxylate group. How does this structure help cartilage resist compression?
o: Its many negative charges repel and hold a large shell of water
Its sugars form covalent cross-links with collagen fibers
Its β(1→4) chains crystallize into rigid, waterproof sheets
Its glycosidic bonds absorb force by breaking and reforming
e: Each repeat carries a –COO⁻, so the chains repel each other and spread out, binding lots of water and counterions.
The resulting hydrated gel pushes back when squeezed and recovers its shape, like a cushion.

q: Which sugar is found in the backbone of DNA?
e: DNA's sugar lacks the –OH at C2′ (deoxy).
RNA uses ribose, which has a 2′-OH.

q: Methyl α-D-glucopyranoside (glucose with –OCH₃ in place of the C1 –OH) does not undergo mutarotation in water. Why?
o: Its C1 is an acetal, so the ring cannot open in water
Its C1 has lost chirality after methylation
Its ring oxygen has been replaced by a carbon
Its C5 –OH is blocked, so it cannot attack C1
e: Mutarotation needs the hemiacetal to open to the free aldehyde and close again.
A glycoside (acetal) is stable in neutral water, so α cannot convert to β; it is also non-reducing.

q: What is the simplest aldose, a three-carbon sugar with one chiral carbon?
e: Glyceraldehyde (HOCH₂–CHOH–CHO) is an aldotriose with one chiral carbon at C2.
Dihydroxyacetone is the simplest ketose and has no chiral carbon; glycerol is not a sugar.
t: D and L sugars are named by comparison with D- and L-glyceraldehyde.

q: In diabetes, blood glucose attaches without any enzyme to the N-terminal valine of hemoglobin's β chains, forming HbA1c, which reflects average blood glucose over about 3 months. Which feature of glucose makes this reaction possible?
o: Its open-chain aldehyde reacts with the amine to form an imine
Its ring hemiacetal –OH forms an ester with valine
Its C6 phosphate forms a salt bridge with the amine
Its glycosidic bond transfers glucose to valine
e: A small fraction of glucose is open-chain, with a free aldehyde at C1.
The aldehyde condenses with the N-terminal –NH₂ to form an imine (Schiff base), which rearranges to a stable product. Higher glucose = more glycation.
t: Glycation (non-enzymatic) ≠ glycosylation (enzyme-controlled).

q: A 3.42 g sample of sucrose (342 g mol⁻¹) is completely hydrolyzed. What total mass of monosaccharides (180 g mol⁻¹ each) forms?
e: Moles of sucrose = 3.42 ÷ 342 = 0.0100 mol; each gives one glucose and one fructose, so 0.0200 mol of monosaccharide.
Mass = 0.0200 × 180 = 3.60 g. It exceeds 3.42 g because hydrolysis adds water (0.0100 mol × 18 = 0.18 g).

q: The liver attaches glucuronic acid (glucose with its C6 –CH₂OH oxidized to –COOH) to many drugs before excretion. Why does this help?
o: Its ionized –COO⁻ and many –OH groups add water solubility
It makes drugs more lipid-soluble to cross membranes
It adds a hydrophobic ring that bile cannot absorb
It turns the drugs into reducing sugars the kidney filters
e: At pH 7.4 the –COOH is ionized (–COO⁻), and the sugar has several polar –OH groups.
The conjugate is much more water-soluble, so it is excreted in urine or bile rather than stored in fat.

q: Reducing D-glucose with NaBH₄ gives one alditol, but reducing D-fructose gives two. Why?
o: Reducing fructose's C2 ketone creates a new chiral center
Fructose's ring opens two ways, giving two ketones
NaBH₄ also removes fructose's C1 –OH as water
Fructose first isomerizes to glucose and galactose
e: Glucose's C1 aldehyde becomes –CH₂OH, which is not chiral: one product (sorbitol).
Fructose's C2 becomes –CHOH– bonded to two different carbons, a new chiral center; hydride adds to either face, giving sorbitol and mannitol.

q: A drop of iodine (I₂ in KI) solution turns deep blue-black on contact with which polysaccharide?
e: Amylose's α(1→4) chain coils into a helix, and iodine ions (such as I₃⁻ and I₅⁻) line up inside it, producing a blue-black color.
Highly branched glycogen has only short helical stretches and gives a red-brown color; cellulose's straight chains give no blue color.

q: Why do cells store glucose as glycogen rather than as an equal mass of free glucose?
o: Glycogen adds little to osmotic pressure, so cells don't swell
Glycogen can be broken down to glucose without any enzymes
Free glucose cannot be phosphorylated inside the cell
Glycogen can diffuse out of cells when blood glucose falls
e: Osmotic pressure depends on the number of dissolved particles, and thousands of glucose units in one glycogen particle count as one particle.
Storing the same glucose free would draw in large amounts of water.

q: Steroid hormones like cortisol travel in the blood bound to carrier proteins. Why?
o: They are hydrophobic and dissolve poorly in plasma
They are too large to fit through capillaries
They would be hydrolyzed by blood enzymes
e: Steroids are lipids and don't dissolve well in water.
Carrier proteins transport them and create a reservoir; only the free fraction is active.

q: People who eat large amounts of fish oil, rich in eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA, a 20-carbon ω-3 fatty acid), tend to have longer bleeding times. Which mechanism best explains this?
o: EPA displaces arachidonate, so weaker thromboxanes form
EPA blocks vitamin K absorption from the intestine
EPA is converted into vitamin K antagonists in the liver
EPA destroys platelets by dissolving their membranes
e: EPA replaces some arachidonic acid (ω-6) in membrane phospholipids and competes for cyclooxygenase.
EPA gives thromboxane A₃, a much weaker platelet activator than thromboxane A₂, so clotting slows.

q: In lipoproteins, much of the cholesterol is esterified to a fatty acid at its C3 hydroxyl. How does this change where it sits in the particle?
o: It becomes more hydrophobic and moves into the core
It becomes more polar and moves to the surface
It gains a negative charge that binds apolipoproteins
It becomes amphipathic and lines the outer shell
e: Free cholesterol's OH lets it sit in the surface monolayer with phospholipids.
Esterifying that OH removes the only polar group, so cholesteryl ester joins TAG in the nonpolar core.

q: Pancreatic lipase removes the fatty acids at glycerol carbons 1 and 3 of a dietary triacylglycerol. What is left for absorption with the free fatty acids?
e: Removing the C1 and C3 fatty acids leaves one fatty acid on C2: 2-monoacylglycerol.
Intestinal cells absorb 2-MAG and fatty acids from micelles and rebuild TAG inside the cell.

q: Which glycerophospholipid is the simplest, with only a phosphate group (and no added head group) on glycerol carbon 3?
e: Phosphatidic acid = glycerol + 2 fatty acids (C1, C2) + phosphate on C3.
Adding a head group (choline, serine, ethanolamine, inositol) to that phosphate gives the other glycerophospholipids; diacylglycerol has no phosphate at all.
t: Phosphatidic acid is the branch point for building both TAGs and phospholipids.

q: Vitamin A is needed for vision because it is converted to:
o: Retinal, the light-absorbing part of rhodopsin
Retinoic acid, which binds opsin to absorb light
A cofactor for carboxylating clotting proteins
e: Light changes 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal, triggering the visual signal.
Deficiency causes night blindness.
w: Retinal, not retinoic acid, absorbs light.

q: Vitamin E's main role in the body is as:
o: A cofactor for carboxylating clotting factors
A hormone that regulates calcium absorption
e: Vitamin E (tocopherol) neutralizes free radicals in membranes, protecting unsaturated fatty acids from oxidation.

q: Phospholipids are amphipathic, which means they:
o: Have both a polar head and nonpolar tails
Are entirely nonpolar along their length
Have a nonpolar head and polar fatty acid tails
Are entirely polar and dissolve freely in water
e: The polar phosphate head faces water; the fatty acid tails avoid it.
This lets phospholipids form bilayers.

q: Vitamin D₃ made in the skin must be hydroxylated twice to become active. In a patient with severe liver failure but normal kidneys, which form is most directly reduced?
o: 25-Hydroxyvitamin D, since the liver adds the 25-OH
7-Dehydrocholesterol, since the liver converts it in skin
Parathyroid hormone, since the liver activates it
Vitamin D₃, since the liver absorbs UV light for the skin
e: The skin converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to vitamin D₃ using UVB; the liver's 25-hydroxylase then makes 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the main circulating form.
The kidney's 1α-hydroxylase finishes the job (calcitriol), so with liver failure the supply of 25-OH-D to the kidney falls first.
t: Skin → liver (25) → kidney (1).

q: Two oils are saponified. Oil A uses more KOH per gram than oil B. What does this best indicate?
o: Oil A's fatty acids are shorter on average
Oil A's fatty acids are longer on average
Oil A's fatty acids have more double bonds
Oil A contains much more free cholesterol
e: Each TAG uses 3 KOH regardless of chain length.
Shorter chains mean a smaller molar mass, so more TAG molecules (and more ester bonds) per gram, which uses more KOH.
t: More base per gram = more ester bonds per gram = shorter chains.

q: Linoleic acid is written 18:2. What does this notation mean?
e: Fatty acid shorthand: number of carbons : number of C=C double bonds.

q: Sphingomyelin is unusual among membrane lipids because it is:
o: Both a sphingolipid and a phospholipid
Both a steroid and a phospholipid
A glycolipid with no phosphate group at all
A glycerolipid with no fatty acid
e: Sphingomyelin is built on sphingosine (so it is a sphingolipid).
Its head group is phosphocholine, so it is also a phospholipid. It is abundant in the myelin sheath.
t: Sphingo- means sphingosine backbone; -myelin hints at where it is concentrated.

q: A snack contains 10 g fat, 20 g carbohydrate and 10 g protein. Using 9, 4 and 4 kcal g⁻¹, about how much energy does it provide?
e: Fat: 10 × 9 = 90 kcal. Carbohydrate: 20 × 4 = 80 kcal. Protein: 10 × 4 = 40 kcal.

q: A person uses about 8,000 kJ of free energy as ATP each day. If each mole of ATP hydrolyzed in cells releases about 50 kJ and ATP's molar mass is about 500 g mol⁻¹, about how much ATP is recycled per day?
e: Moles of ATP = 8000 kJ ÷ 50 kJ mol⁻¹ = 160 mol.
Mass = 160 mol × 0.5 kg mol⁻¹ = 80 kg.
The body holds only a small ATP pool at any moment, so each ATP is regenerated hundreds of times a day.

q: Why does the actual ΔG of a reaction in a cell often differ from its ΔG°′?
o: Real cellular concentrations differ from standard conditions
Enzymes in the cell change the reaction's free energy change
Cells are much colder than the standard temperature of 25 °C
ΔG°′ applies only to gas-phase reactions, not to solutions
e: ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q.
Cells keep products low or reactants high, shifting ΔG.

q: In a patient with insulin resistance, a brisk 30-minute walk lowers blood glucose even though insulin signaling in muscle is impaired. What best explains this?
o: Rising AMP activates AMPK, which moves GLUT4 to the membrane without insulin
Exercise raises glucagon, which makes skeletal muscle take up glucose
Exercise releases insulin that is stored inside the muscle fibers
Contraction makes the liver convert blood glucose into glycogen
e: Contracting muscle uses ATP, so AMP rises and activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK).
AMPK (along with Ca²⁺ signals) moves GLUT4 to the muscle surface through a pathway independent of the insulin receptor.
This is one reason exercise helps control blood glucose in type 2 diabetes.

q: Glucagon's main effect is to:
o: Raise blood glucose via liver glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis
Lower blood glucose via liver glycogen synthesis and glucose uptake
Raise blood glucose via muscle glycogen breakdown and glucose release
Lower blood glucose by increasing GLUT4 uptake in muscle and fat
e: Glucagon (from α cells) is the main fasting hormone.

q: During a long fast, the body's fuel sources change over time. Which order is correct?
o: Liver glycogen → gluconeogenesis rises → ketone bodies become major fuel
Ketone bodies → liver glycogen is used → gluconeogenesis rises
Muscle protein → liver glycogen → fat stores become major fuel
Liver glycogen → ketone bodies become major fuel → gluconeogenesis rises
e: Liver glycogen lasts roughly a day.
Gluconeogenesis rises (from amino acids, lactate, glycerol).
After several days, ketone bodies from fat become a major fuel, sparing protein.

q: Many biosynthetic reactions split ATP into AMP + PPi, after which pyrophosphatase rapidly hydrolyzes PPi to 2 Pi. What is the purpose of the second step?
o: Removing PPi makes the overall reaction strongly favorable and essentially irreversible
PPi hydrolysis regenerates the ATP that the first step used, so no energy is spent
PPi is toxic to the enzyme, which would be inhibited permanently if PPi remained
Pyrophosphatase transfers the phosphate onto the product to form the final compound
e: PPi hydrolysis has ΔG°′ ≈ −19 kJ mol⁻¹, and keeping [PPi] very low pulls the first reaction forward.
Examples include fatty acid activation, UDP-glucose formation and DNA synthesis; such steps cost 2 ATP equivalents.
t: PPi → 2 Pi is the cell's ratchet: it makes activation steps one-way.

q: In a cell at 37 °C (RT ≈ 2.6 kJ mol⁻¹), a reaction has K′<sub>eq</sub> = 1000 and mass-action ratio Q = 10. What is ΔG? (ln 0.01 ≈ −4.6)
e: = 2.6 × (−4.6) ≈ −12 kJ mol⁻¹. Q < K, so the reaction proceeds forward.
t: Using log₁₀ instead of ln gives the −5 trap (2.6 × −2).
w: Q is below K, so ΔG is negative.

q: Phosphoglucose isomerase converts glucose-6-phosphate to fructose-6-phosphate with ΔG°′ = +1.7 kJ mol⁻¹. Using ΔG°′ = −RT ln K′<sub>eq</sub> (RT ≈ 2.5 kJ mol⁻¹, e<sup>−0.7</sup> ≈ 0.5), what is K′<sub>eq</sub> for this step?
e: K′<sub>eq</sub> = e<sup>−0.7</sup> ≈ 0.5: at equilibrium, fructose-6-phosphate is about half as abundant as glucose-6-phosphate. A small positive ΔG°′ means K′<sub>eq</sub> slightly below 1.

q: In a cell at 37 °C (RT ≈ 2.6 kJ mol⁻¹), [ATP] = 5 mM, [ADP] = 0.5 mM and [Pi] = 5 mM. Given ΔG°′ = −30.5 kJ mol⁻¹ for ATP hydrolysis and ln(5 × 10⁻⁴) ≈ −7.6, what is the actual ΔG?
e: ΔG = −30.5 + 2.6 × (−7.6) ≈ −30.5 − 19.8 ≈ −50 kJ mol⁻¹. Keeping ATP far above ADP makes hydrolysis much more favorable than under standard conditions.
t: Cells keep ATP far from equilibrium, so its real ΔG (about −50) beats the textbook −30.5.

q: Standard biochemical conditions (used for ΔG°′) differ from chemical standard conditions (ΔG°) mainly in that:
o: All solutes are 1 M except H⁺, which is 10⁻⁷ M (pH 7)
All solutes, including H⁺, are 1 M, so the pH is 0
All solutes are held at typical cellular levels at 37 °C
All solutes are 1 mM, at pH 7.4 and body temperature
e: Both use 1 M solutes, 1 atm and a stated temperature (usually 25 °C).
ΔG°′ fixes [H⁺] at 10⁻⁷ M (pH 7), which suits reactions in cells; water's concentration is also treated as constant.
t: The prime (′) means pH 7: biochemists' standard state.

q: In the first seconds of intense exercise, which compound regenerates ATP in skeletal muscle by transferring its phosphate directly to ADP?
e: Creatine kinase catalyzes phosphocreatine + ADP → creatine + ATP.
Phosphocreatine's phosphate-transfer potential (ΔG°′ of hydrolysis ≈ −43 kJ mol⁻¹) is higher than ATP's (≈ −30.5), so the transfer is favorable.
This buffer lasts only seconds, until glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation speed up.
t: Phosphocreatine is muscle's ATP 'battery': first to be used, quickly emptied.

q: The four tripeptides in the table are spotted at the center of a paper strip in a buffer at pH 6.0, and a voltage is applied. Which moves fastest toward the anode (+)?
e: Every peptide has a free N-terminus (+1) and C-terminus (−1) at pH 6, so the side chains decide the net charge.
W: Asp and Glu side chains are both −1, so net −2, the most negative. X is +1 (Lys), Y is 0, and Z is about +½ (His, pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 6).
t: Anode = positive electrode, which attracts negative species. 'An ox' (anode = oxidation) pulls anions.

q: Glycine (pK<sub>a</sub> 2.3 for –COOH and 9.6 for –NH₃⁺) is drawn in the form shown. In which solution is this the main form?
o: pH 1, where its net charge is +1
pH 6, where its net charge is 0
pH 12, where its net charge is −1
pH 6, where its net charge is +1
e: The drawn form has –NH₃⁺ and an un-ionized –COOH, so its net charge is +1.
Both groups are protonated only when pH is below 2.3, so pH 1 fits.

q: Three patients lack activity of the same enzyme. Their mRNA and protein results are shown. Which set of mutations best explains the data?
e: Patient 1 makes normal amounts of normal-sized protein that doesn't work: an amino acid change (missense) in a key residue.
No mRNA (patient 2) points to failed transcription (promoter); longer mRNA (patient 3) fits an intron left in by a splice-site defect.

q: Based on the melting points shown, which conclusion is best supported?
o: One cis double bond lowers the melting point far more than two fewer carbons
Chain length matters far more than the number of cis double bonds
Each added cis double bond raises the melting point by about 20 °C
Lauric acid would be a liquid at room temperature (25 °C)
e: Removing 2 carbons (stearic → palmitic) drops the melting point 70 − 63 = 7 °C.
Adding one cis double bond (stearic → oleic) drops it 70 − 13 = 57 °C; lauric (44 °C) is still solid at 25 °C.

q: A secreted protein runs at about 66 kDa on SDS-PAGE. After treatment with PNGase F, an enzyme that removes sugar chains attached to asparagine side chains, it runs at about 52 kDa (gel shown). What does this show?
o: About 14 kDa of its apparent mass was N-linked carbohydrate
About 14 kDa of O-linked sugar was attached to Ser and Thr
It had a 14 kDa subunit held on by a disulfide bond
PNGase F cut the polypeptide chain into smaller pieces
e: Sugars attached to Asn N atoms are N-linked; removing them drops the mass by 66 − 52 = 14 kDa.
The protein remains a single band, so the chain itself wasn't cut, and no reducing agent was involved.

q: Using the Lineweaver–Burk plot shown, what are the enzyme's V<sub>max</sub> and K<sub>m</sub>?
e: The y-intercept is 1/V<sub>max</sub> = 0.05 s µM⁻¹, so V<sub>max</sub> = 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20 µM s⁻¹.
The x-intercept is −1/K<sub>m</sub> = −0.25 mM⁻¹, so K<sub>m</sub> = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4 mM.
t: Every intercept on a double-reciprocal plot is a reciprocal. Flip it before you report it.

q: A young adult has muscle pain and dark urine (myoglobin) after long exercise or fasting. Tests of fatty acid oxidation are shown. Octanoate enters mitochondria without carnitine. Which step is most likely defective?
o: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II, on the matrix side
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I, on the outer membrane
Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase in the matrix
Thiolase, the final step of every β-oxidation round
e: Octanoate oxidation is normal (98%), so β-oxidation enzymes inside the matrix, including those for medium chains, work.
Palmitoylcarnitine bypasses CPT-I, yet its oxidation is still low (12%), so the block is at CPT-II, which converts acylcarnitine back to acyl-CoA in the matrix.
