q: In Gibson and Walk's visual cliff studies, most crawling infants (about 6–14 months old) would not cross onto the glass over the 'deep' side, even when their mothers called. Why can't this result alone prove that depth perception is innate?
o: The infants had months of visual experience before testing
The infants could feel the glass, so vision was irrelevant
The mothers' calls made the infants too anxious to move
Too few infants were tested to support any conclusion
e: Infants can't be tested until they can crawl, and by then they have had months to learn about depth.
So the study shows depth perception is present by crawling age, not that it was there at birth.

q: A patient whose cochlear hair cells were destroyed by a toxic antibiotic receives a cochlear implant. The device restores some hearing because it:
o: Stimulates the auditory nerve directly with electrodes
Amplifies sound so the remaining hair cells respond
Replaces the small bones of the middle ear
Sends sound vibrations through the skull bones
e: Losing hair cells causes sensorineural hearing loss, so making sound louder doesn't help much.
The implant bypasses hair cells: electrodes along the cochlea stimulate auditory nerve fibers, with different positions signaling different pitches (place coding).

q: After staring at a red image, a person sees a green afterimage on a white wall. Which theory best explains this?
e: Red–green, blue–yellow and black–white work as opposing pairs.
Fatigue on one side produces the opposite color when it rebounds.

q: A cook barely notices adding 1 g of salt to 50 g of seasoning. According to Weber's law, how much must be added to 200 g to be noticed?
e: The JND is a constant proportion: 1/50 = 2%.

q: In a hearing test, a patient says "I hear a tone" on a trial when no tone was played. In signal detection theory, this response is a:
e: Signal absent + response "yes" = false alarm.
Signal present + "yes" = hit; signal present + "no" = miss.
Signal absent + "no" = correct rejection.
t: Draw the 2 × 2 grid (signal present/absent × yes/no). It answers every version of this question.
w: A hit needs a real signal.
A miss is saying no to a real signal.
Correct rejection is saying no to no signal.

q: The semicircular canals detect:
e: They're part of the vestibular system, which supports balance.

q: In what order does a visual signal pass through the cells of the retina on its way to the brain?
e: Rods and cones transduce light, then signal bipolar cells, which signal ganglion cells.
Ganglion cell axons bundle into the optic nerve.
t: Trap: light physically passes through the ganglion and bipolar layers first, but the neural SIGNAL starts at the photoreceptors.

q: A patient with a growing pituitary tumor keeps bumping into door frames on both sides, though his central vision is clear. The tumor presses upward on the middle of the optic chiasm. Which visual field loss is expected?
o: Loss of the outer (temporal) half of each eye's visual field
Complete blindness in one eye, while the other eye stays normal
Loss of the left half of the visual field in both eyes
Loss of the inner (nasal) half of each eye's visual field
e: At the optic chiasm, only fibers from the nasal (inner) half of each retina cross.
The nasal retina receives light from the temporal (outer) visual field, so pressing on the crossing fibers causes bitemporal hemianopia, or 'tunnel vision.'
t: Nasal retina sees the temporal field: retina and field are mirror images.

q: In a hearing test, a patient says 'yes' often, catching every real tone but also giving many false alarms. In signal detection terms, this person has:
e: A liberal criterion means a willingness to say 'yes' even when unsure.
Sensitivity (d′) and response bias are separate.

q: A person can just barely tell that a 100 g weight is heavier when 2 g is added. According to Weber's law, about how much must be added to a 500 g weight to notice a difference?
e: Weber's law: the just-noticeable difference (JND) is a constant fraction of the original stimulus.
Here the fraction is 2 g ÷ 100 g = 2%.
t: Weber's law is a proportion problem. Find the fraction first, then scale it.

q: A man lacks working medium-wavelength ('green') cones and confuses reds with greens, yet his vision is otherwise normal. Which theory does his condition most directly support?
e: Trichromatic (Young–Helmholtz) theory says color vision depends on three cone types.
Missing one type leaves only two (dichromacy), which predicts exactly this kind of color confusion.

q: Which vestibular structures detect linear acceleration and head tilt relative to gravity, as when an elevator starts to rise?
o: The ossicles of the middle ear
e: The utricle and saccule contain hair cells covered by tiny crystals (otoliths) that shift with gravity and straight-line acceleration.
The semicircular canals detect rotation; the cochlea is for hearing.

q: After a concussion, a football player cannot remember the 30 minutes before the hit, but his memories from the previous week and from childhood are intact. What does this pattern suggest?
o: His most recent memories had not yet been fully consolidated
He has anterograde amnesia from hippocampal removal
His older memories are held in sensory memory
His older memories are held in short-term memory
e: Losing memories from before an injury is retrograde amnesia.
Recent memories are lost first because consolidation into stable long-term storage takes time; older memories are more resistant.

q: A patient feels nauseated every time she smells the hospital where she received chemotherapy. In classical conditioning terms, the hospital smell is the:
e: The chemotherapy naturally causes nausea: unconditioned stimulus → unconditioned response.
The smell was paired with chemotherapy and now triggers nausea on its own.
A once-neutral cue that now triggers a learned response is the conditioned stimulus. The nausea to the smell is the conditioned response.
t: Ask: did this need to be learned? If yes, it's 'conditioned'.
w: Nausea to the chemo is the unconditioned response.
Nausea to the smell is the conditioned response.

q: Habituation is:
o: A decreased response to a repeated, harmless stimulus
An increased response after a painful stimulus
e: Example: no longer startling at a fan's noise.

q: Participants verify 'A canary can sing' faster than 'A canary has skin.' According to Collins and Quillian's hierarchical network model of semantic memory, why?
o: 'Has skin' is stored at a more distant level (animal)
'Has skin' is a false statement about canaries
Shorter sentences are always verified faster
Singing is stored in procedural memory instead
e: The model stores each property at the most general level that it applies to: 'can sing' with canary, 'can fly' with bird, 'has skin' with animal.
Verifying 'has skin' requires moving up two levels in the network, which takes extra time.

q: In 1956, George Miller proposed that short-term memory holds about how many items (or chunks) at once?
e: Miller's 'magical number seven, plus or minus two' described short-term memory span.
Some later researchers argue the true limit is closer to 4 chunks, but 7 ± 2 is the classic figure.

q: A teenager comes home after curfew, so his parents take away his car keys for a week, and he stops coming home late. This is:
e: Something desirable (car access) is REMOVED, so it is negative.
The late behavior DECREASES, so it is punishment.
t: Positive/negative = add/remove; reinforcement/punishment = behavior goes up/down.

q: A child bitten by one dog becomes afraid of all dogs. This is:
e: The response spreads to stimuli similar to the original conditioned stimulus.

q: A factory worker is paid $5 for every 10 garments she finishes. Which reinforcement schedule is this?
e: Reinforcement comes after a set NUMBER of responses (10 garments), so it is a ratio schedule.
The number never changes, so it is fixed. Fixed-ratio schedules produce high response rates with short pauses after each reward.

q: Wolfgang Köhler's chimpanzee Sultan failed to reach bananas outside his cage with one short stick. After a pause, he suddenly fitted two sticks together and raked the bananas in. This is an example of:
e: Insight learning is the sudden realization of a solution, often after a pause, rather than gradual trial and error.
Shaping and conditioning build behavior step by step through experience.

q: After extinction, a conditioned response suddenly returns following a rest period. This is:
e: The learning wasn't erased, only suppressed.

q: Eyewitnesses who heard the word 'smashed' estimated higher car speeds than those who heard 'hit'. This illustrates:
e: Information after an event can change how the event is remembered.

q: Rats drank sweet water while each lick also triggered a flash of light and a click. Then one group was made ill by X-ray exposure, and another received foot shocks. Later, the ill rats avoided the sweet taste but not the light and click, while the shocked rats avoided the light and click but not the taste. What does this show?
o: Animals are biologically prepared to link certain cues to certain outcomes
Any stimulus can be paired equally well with any consequence at all
Taste aversions need many separate pairings before they appear
Rats cannot detect lights and sounds while they are drinking
e: If all pairings were equal, each group would avoid both the taste and the light-and-click.
Instead, taste was linked to illness and light-and-click to pain, so evolution has prepared some associations (Garcia and Koelling's finding).
t: Taste goes with nausea; sights and sounds go with pain.

q: An EEG shows mostly high-amplitude, low-frequency delta waves. The sleeper is most likely in:
e: Delta waves are the slowest, largest brain waves.
They define stage N3, also called slow-wave or deep sleep.
REM sleep looks like a waking EEG (fast, low-amplitude beta-like waves).
t: N2 has sleep spindles and K-complexes. N3 has delta waves. REM has vivid dreams and muscle paralysis.
w: REM looks like a waking EEG.

q: A patient after a stroke speaks slowly in short, effortful phrases but understands what others say. Which brain area was most likely damaged?
e: Broca's area (frontal lobe) is involved in speech production.
Damage causes non-fluent (Broca's) aphasia, with comprehension mostly spared.
Wernicke's aphasia is the opposite: fluent speech that makes little sense, with poor comprehension.
t: Broca's = Broken speech. Wernicke's = Wordy but makes no sense.

q: A theorist argues that a gifted dancer, a skilled counselor and a math prodigy each show a different kind of intelligence that IQ tests miss. This view best matches:
e: Gardner proposed several separate intelligences, such as bodily-kinesthetic, interpersonal and logical-mathematical.
Spearman instead argued that one general factor (g) underlies performance on all mental tests.

q: In Piaget's three-mountain task, a 4-year-old is asked what a doll on the far side of a mountain model can see, and she describes her own view. This reflects:
o: Missing object permanence in the sensorimotor stage
Failed conservation in the formal operational stage
Abstract reasoning in the concrete operational stage
e: Preoperational children (about ages 2–7) have trouble taking another person's point of view.
Describing her own view as the doll's shows egocentrism.

q: A student who scrolls on her phone in bed until 1 a.m. has trouble falling asleep. Which explanation is best supported by research on circadian rhythms?
o: Bright, blue-rich light suppresses evening melatonin release
Screen light raises melatonin and causes REM rebound
Darkness signals the SCN to stop releasing melatonin
Phone use causes narcolepsy-like sleep attacks
e: Light-sensitive retinal ganglion cells, most responsive to blue light, signal the SCN.
The SCN then suppresses melatonin from the pineal gland, delaying the body's 'time to sleep' signal.

q: A clinician reasons: 'All patients with this mutation develop the disease. This patient has the mutation. So this patient will develop the disease.' This is:
e: Deductive reasoning moves from general premises to a specific, logically certain conclusion.
Inductive reasoning goes the other way, building a general rule from specific cases.

q: A person with narcolepsy:
o: Suddenly falls asleep during the day, sometimes entering REM directly
Has persistent trouble falling asleep or staying asleep at night
Repeatedly stops breathing during sleep and wakes briefly each time
Acts out vivid dreams because the normal muscle paralysis of REM fails
e: Narcolepsy can include cataplexy (sudden muscle weakness).

q: Which drug class slows central nervous system activity?
e: Depressants often enhance GABA activity.

q: Chomsky's sentence 'Colorless green ideas sleep furiously' sounds grammatical to English speakers even though it means nothing. It shows that:
o: Syntax can be judged separately from meaning
Meaning is needed to judge whether grammar is correct
Phonemes carry the meaning of whole sentences
Language determines how speakers perceive colors
e: Syntax is the set of rules for combining words; semantics is meaning.
The sentence follows English word-order rules but makes no sense, so people can judge grammar without meaning.

q: According to the activation-synthesis hypothesis, dreams are:
o: The brain's attempt to interpret random neural activity in REM
Disguised expressions of unconscious wishes and conflicts
A process for consolidating memories from the previous day
Mental rehearsal of threats to prepare for waking life
e: Freud's theory, by contrast, sees dreams as disguised wishes.

q: As a person drifts from relaxed wakefulness into stage N1 sleep, which EEG waves become most prominent?
e: Relaxed, eyes-closed wakefulness shows alpha waves.
In N1 these give way to slower theta waves; delta waves appear later, in N3.
t: Order of slowing: Beta (alert) → Alpha (relaxed) → Theta (N1) → Delta (N3): 'BAT-D'.

q: According to Piaget, a child who understands that pouring water into a taller glass doesn't change its amount has reached the:
e: Conservation develops around ages 7–11.

q: Which lobe of the brain contains the primary visual cortex?
e: Visual information is processed first in the occipital lobe at the back of the brain.

q: A patient has trouble recognizing familiar faces but can recognize people by their voices. Damage to which area is most likely?
o: Broca's area (left inferior frontal lobe region)
e: This condition is called prosopagnosia.
The fusiform face area is specialized for face recognition.

q: Stroking the sole of a 3-month-old's foot makes her big toe extend upward and her other toes fan out (the Babinski sign). If an adult showed this same response, it would most likely indicate:
o: Damage to the motor pathway from the brain
A normal, fully mature spinal reflex
Overactive pain receptors in the foot
Damage limited to receptors in the skin
e: In infants the corticospinal (motor) tracts are still maturing, so the Babinski sign is normal.
In healthy adults the toes curl downward; an upward big toe signals damage to the motor pathway from the brain (upper motor neurons).
t: Babinski: normal in babies, a red flag in adults.

q: Adoption studies are useful in behavioral genetics because they:
o: Separate genes (from biological parents) from environment (from adoptive parents)
Show that the shared rearing environment is the main source of traits
Hold genes constant by studying only adopted identical twin pairs
Remove all environmental effects so that genetic effects can be measured directly
e: Comparing adopted children to both sets of parents helps tease apart nature and nurture.

q: Which brain imaging technique best shows which brain regions are active during a task?
e: fMRI tracks changes in blood oxygen (BOLD signal) that follow neural activity.
CT and structural MRI mainly show anatomy.

q: A cook touches a hot pan and jerks her hand away before she feels any pain. Why does the movement come before the sensation?
o: The withdrawal reflex loops through the spinal cord without waiting for the brain
Pain receptors in the skin also contract the arm muscles directly
The brain decides to move first and creates the pain afterward
Pain signals travel faster than motor signals to the arm
e: In a withdrawal reflex, sensory neurons enter the spinal cord, where interneurons immediately activate the motor neurons that pull the arm away.
The pain signal has to travel up to the brain and be processed before it is felt, which takes longer. So the hand is already moving by the time she notices the pain.
t: Reflexes are wired in the spinal cord; feeling needs the brain.

q: Brain scans of experienced London taxi drivers, who memorize the city's complex street layout, showed larger posterior hippocampi than in controls, and size increased with years on the job. This best supports:
o: Experience-driven plasticity in a region used for spatial memory
Hippocampal size is fixed by genes before adulthood
The hippocampus controls the motor skills of driving
Spatial memory is stored mainly in the cerebellum
e: The hippocampus is important for spatial navigation and memory.
Because size grew with years of driving, the finding suggests that heavy use can reshape brain structure (neuroplasticity), although the study is correlational.

q: Neurons in the locus coeruleus of the pons project widely through the brain and become very active during alertness and stress. Which neurotransmitter do they mainly release?
e: The locus coeruleus is the brain's main source of norepinephrine, which raises arousal and vigilance.
For comparison: raphe nuclei → serotonin; substantia nigra and VTA → dopamine.
t: Locus coeruleus = 'blue spot' = norepinephrine alarm center.

q: Which division of the nervous system controls voluntary skeletal muscle movement?
e: Somatic motor neurons innervate skeletal muscle.
w: The enteric system runs the gut.

q: A patient has damage to the reticular formation in the brainstem. Which problem is most likely?
o: Impaired wakefulness and arousal, possibly coma
Inability to form new explicit memories of events
Loss of fine coordination of movement
e: The reticular formation (reticular activating system) projects through the thalamus to the cortex and keeps the brain alert.
Damage can reduce arousal and even cause coma. Faces depend on the fusiform gyrus, new memories on the hippocampus and coordination on the cerebellum.

q: In a long-term New Zealand study, Caspi and colleagues reported that people carrying one or two short versions of a serotonin transporter gene variant were more likely to become depressed after many stressful life events than people with two long versions. With few stressful events, depression rates were similar. What does this pattern illustrate?
o: A purely genetic cause of depression
A purely environmental cause of depression
e: The gene variant mattered mainly when stress was high, and stress mattered more for people with the short variant.
When the effect of one factor depends on the level of another, that is an interaction. (Later attempts to replicate this specific finding have had mixed results.)

q: Researchers apply transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over a volunteer's left motor cortex, and her right thumb twitches. What key advantage does TMS have over fMRI for studying brain function?
o: It alters brain activity directly, so it can test causation
It measures blood flow more precisely than fMRI
It records single neurons directly through the intact skull
It gives detailed images of brain structure
e: fMRI shows which areas are active during a task, which is correlational.
TMS briefly excites or disrupts a cortical area; if behavior changes, that area plays a causal role.

q: In Selye's general adaptation syndrome, which stage comes after alarm?
e: Alarm → resistance → exhaustion.
Long-term stress depletes the body's resources.

q: Which brain structure, besides the amygdala, is especially important in regulating emotion through planning and reasoning?
e: The prefrontal cortex helps control emotional reactions and impulses.

q: The Cannon–Bard theory says that:
o: Arousal and emotional experience occur simultaneously and independently
Emotional experience follows from the perception of bodily arousal
Emotion results from arousal plus a cognitive label for it
Emotion begins with a cognitive appraisal before any arousal
e: The thalamus sends signals to the cortex and body at once.

q: A patient with an incurable illness cannot change her diagnosis, so she practices meditation, journals and focuses on the meaning she finds in her family. This is an example of:
e: Emotion-focused coping manages the emotional response to a stressor rather than changing the stressor itself.
It is especially useful when the stressor cannot be controlled, as with an incurable diagnosis.

q: Salmon swim upstream to spawn in the stream where they hatched, without ever being taught. Which theory of motivation explains behavior as driven by inborn, unlearned patterns like this?
e: Instinct theory (associated with William James and William McDougall) says behavior is driven by innate, species-typical patterns.
The salmon's spawning run is fixed and unlearned, which is exactly what an instinct is.
t: Instinct theory fits animals well but explains little human behavior, which is why later theories replaced it.

q: Psychologists commonly describe an emotion as having which three components?
e: An emotion includes a physiological component (bodily arousal), a behavioral component (expressions and actions) and a cognitive component (the subjective feeling and appraisal).
Alarm, resistance and exhaustion are the stages of Selye's general adaptation syndrome, not parts of an emotion.

q: A man with chronic knee pain must choose between a painful surgery with months of rehabilitation and continuing to live with the pain. He strongly dislikes both options. This is which type of conflict?
e: Both choices are unpleasant, so he is stuck between two things he wants to avoid.
This conflict often causes stalling, because moving toward either option makes it feel worse.
t: Professor Tip: 'lesser of two evils' = avoidance–avoidance.

q: A long-term heroin user who always injects in the same room takes his usual dose in an unfamiliar place and nearly dies of an overdose. Shepard Siegel explained cases like this with which idea?
o: Familiar cues trigger a learned compensatory response that is absent in a new setting
The drug is chemically stronger when it is taken in an unfamiliar place
Withdrawal symptoms are always more severe in new environments
Tolerance depends only on liver enzymes, so the setting cannot matter
e: Through classical conditioning, cues in the usual setting come to trigger body changes that oppose the drug's effect, which is part of tolerance.
In a new place those cues are absent, so the usual dose hits with less opposition and can be fatal.
t: Part of tolerance is learned and tied to the setting.

q: A retired surgeon has a stable income, a loving family and the respect of her colleagues. She now spends her time learning to paint, wanting to reach her full creative potential. According to Maslow, which need is she pursuing?
e: Her physiological, safety, belonging and esteem needs are already met.
Striving to fulfill one's full potential is self-actualization, the top of Maslow's hierarchy.

q: In Lazarus's appraisal model, secondary appraisal is:
o: Judging whether you have the resources to cope with a stressor
Judging whether a situation is threatening or harmless
Reassessing a stressor after an initial coping attempt
The body's alarm reaction during the first stage of stress
e: Primary appraisal: Is this a threat? Secondary appraisal: Can I handle it?

q: Drive-reduction theory proposes that behavior is motivated by:
o: A desire to reduce internal tension from unmet biological needs
A desire to maintain an optimal, moderate level of arousal
Innate, fixed behavior patterns shaped by evolution
The pull of external incentives such as money, grades or praise
e: Hunger creates a drive; eating reduces it, restoring homeostasis.

q: Which brain structure, rich in receptors for cortisol, is especially vulnerable to damage from long-term high cortisol levels during chronic stress?
e: The hippocampus has many glucocorticoid receptors and helps shut off the HPA axis through negative feedback.
Prolonged high cortisol is linked to shrinking of hippocampal neurons and to memory problems.

q: Agoraphobia is best described as intense fear of:
o: Situations where escape or help might be hard to get
Being judged or embarrassed by other people
One specific object or animal, such as spiders or dogs
e: Agoraphobia is fear and avoidance of places like crowds, public transport or open spaces because escape might be difficult if panic-like symptoms occur.
Fear of judgment is social anxiety disorder; fear of one object is a specific phobia.

q: Repeated unwanted thoughts that cause anxiety, and rituals done to reduce it, describe:
e: Obsessions are thoughts; compulsions are actions.

q: The diathesis–stress model proposes that disorders develop when:
o: An underlying vulnerability interacts with stressful life events
Enough stress causes a disorder regardless of vulnerability
A genetic vulnerability causes a disorder regardless of stress
Learned helplessness develops after uncontrollable events
e: Diathesis = predisposition (genetic or psychological).

q: Unstable relationships, self-image and emotions, along with intense fear of abandonment, describe:
e: Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) was developed for this disorder.

q: After a frightening argument, a patient suddenly cannot move her right arm. Neurological testing finds no damage, and the symptom does not fit any known neurological disease. DSM-5-TR calls this:
e: Functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder) involves motor or sensory symptoms that are incompatible with recognized neurological conditions.
In factitious disorder, symptoms are deliberately faked; here they are not intentionally produced.

q: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) work by:
o: Blocking serotonin reuptake, so more serotonin stays in the synapse
Blocking serotonin receptors, so less serotonin signal is received
Inhibiting the enzyme that breaks down serotonin and other monoamines
Increasing serotonin release from presynaptic vesicles
e: SSRIs (like fluoxetine) are used for depression and anxiety disorders.

q: After David Rosenhan's 1973 pseudopatient study, one hospital was told that fake patients would try to get admitted over the next 3 months. Staff rated 41 of 193 new admissions as likely pseudopatients, but Rosenhan had sent none. What does this follow-up most directly suggest?
o: Staff could not reliably tell real patients from healthy people in this setting
Staff were able to spot every pseudopatient once they were warned
Most of the 193 new admissions were healthy people faking symptoms
Diagnostic labels have no effect on how staff interpret behavior
e: When staff expected fakes, they labeled real patients as fakes; in the first study, they had labeled healthy people as ill.
Both errors suggest the diagnoses depended heavily on context and expectation. The study was influential, though later researchers have questioned parts of its methods and data.

q: Which is a negative symptom of schizophrenia?
e: Negative symptoms are reductions in normal function: flat affect, alogia (little speech), avolition (low motivation).

q: The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia proposes:
o: Too much dopamine activity in certain brain pathways
Too little dopamine activity throughout the brain
Too little serotonin activity in mood-related pathways
Too much GABA activity in the prefrontal cortex
e: Antipsychotics that block dopamine D₂ receptors reduce positive symptoms.

q: Bipolar I disorder is defined by:
e: Mania: elevated mood, little need for sleep, racing thoughts, risky behavior.
Bipolar II involves hypomania and depression.

q: Which is a key feature of dissociative identity disorder?
o: Two or more distinct identity states
e: It's often linked to severe childhood trauma. It isn't the same as schizophrenia.

q: How does illness anxiety disorder differ from somatic symptom disorder?
o: Illness anxiety involves few or no symptoms but heavy fear of illness
Illness anxiety involves many symptoms but no worry about them
Illness anxiety is always caused by a real medical disease
Illness anxiety involves faking symptoms for money or benefits
e: In illness anxiety disorder, physical symptoms are absent or mild, but the person is preoccupied with having or getting a serious illness.
In somatic symptom disorder, distressing physical symptoms are present and the person's thoughts and feelings about them are excessive.

q: After a new baby sister arrives, a 5-year-old who was fully toilet trained starts wetting the bed and asking for a bottle. Which defense mechanism does this illustrate?
e: Regression is returning to behavior from an earlier stage of development when under stress.
The older child falls back to infant-like behaviors after the sibling's arrival.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes suppression from repression?
o: Suppression is conscious; repression is unconscious
Repression is conscious; suppression is unconscious
Both are conscious forms of forgetting on purpose
Both are unconscious and work in exactly the same way
e: Repression is an unconscious defense that keeps threatening thoughts out of awareness.
Suppression is a deliberate, conscious choice to push a thought aside, like deciding not to think about a bill until after an exam.
t: Suppression = you Shove it aside on purpose (conscious); Repression = Removed from awareness without your knowledge (unconscious).

q: Self-esteem refers to:
o: A person's overall evaluation of their own worth
A person's belief they can succeed at a task
A person's knowledge of their various social roles
A person's sense that others control their fate
e: Self-esteem is evaluative: how positively or negatively you view yourself.
Belief in your ability at a specific task is self-efficacy, and the last option describes an external locus of control.

q: At work, at parties and with family, a man carefully watches others and changes how he acts to fit what each situation seems to call for. He is best described as:
e: Mark Snyder's self-monitoring describes how much people adjust their behavior to social cues.
High self-monitors adapt to each setting; low self-monitors act on their inner attitudes and stay consistent.

q: Kohlberg's postconventional stage is shown when someone says:
o: 'Laws should be broken if they violate basic human rights.'
'I'll do it so I don't get punished.'
'I'll follow the rules so people think I'm good.'
'Rules must always be followed to keep order.'
e: Postconventional reasoning appeals to universal principles.

q: Hazel Markus and Paula Nurius proposed that 'possible selves'—images of who we hope to become and who we fear becoming—mainly serve to:
o: Motivate and guide behavior toward future goals
Defend the ego against anxiety from the id
Store memories of past events in order
Fix personality permanently by early childhood
e: A hoped-for self (a future doctor) pulls behavior toward a goal, and a feared self (failing out) pushes behavior away from it.
Possible selves link the self-concept to motivation.

q: Gordon Allport described a single trait so dominant that it shapes nearly everything a person does, such as a lifelong devotion to helping the poor. He called this a:
e: Allport ranked traits as cardinal (rare, all-encompassing), central (the handful of main traits) and secondary (situation-specific preferences).
Source traits are a term from Raymond Cattell, not Allport.

q: Erikson's final stage, in late adulthood, is:
e: Older adults reflect on whether life was meaningful.

q: Self-concept refers to:
o: Your overall set of beliefs about who you are
Your overall positive or negative evaluation of your worth
Your belief in your ability to succeed
The way others actually perceive you
e: Self-esteem is your evaluation of yourself; self-concept is your description.

q: Channeling aggressive urges into playing football is an example of:
e: Sublimation turns unacceptable impulses into socially acceptable activities.

q: Carl Rogers believed people develop best when they receive:
e: Rogers was a humanistic psychologist; acceptance helps the self-concept grow.

q: Bandura's concept of reciprocal determinism says behavior results from interactions among:
o: Unconscious drives of the id, ego and superego
e: Each factor affects the others.

q: A smoker who knows smoking causes cancer tells himself, "My grandfather smoked and lived to 95." This is an attempt to reduce:
e: Cognitive dissonance is discomfort from holding conflicting beliefs and behaviors.
Smoking conflicts with knowing that smoking is dangerous.
He reduces the conflict by adding a belief that minimizes the danger.
t: People reduce dissonance by changing the behavior OR changing the belief. Changing the belief is usually easier.
w: Learned helplessness is giving up after no control.
The just-world bias is about deserved outcomes.
Role strain is tension within one role.

q: After spending an hour on a very boring task, participants paid $1 to tell others it was fun rated the task as more enjoyable than those paid $20. Why?
o: Low pay caused more dissonance, so they changed their attitude to fit the lie
Higher pay caused more dissonance, so those participants disliked the task
Low pay made the task feel harder, so they valued their effort more
Higher pay made participants feel guilty, so they rated the task lower
e: Festinger and Carlsmith's classic study.
Large pay gave an external justification; small pay didn't.

q: In a dark room, a still point of light appears to move (the autokinetic effect). Muzafer Sherif found that people estimating the movement in groups gradually converged on a shared estimate, and they kept using it when later tested alone. What does this show?
o: Groups create norms in ambiguous situations, and people internalize them
People ignore others when a task is uncertain and rely on themselves
Conformity happens only when the correct answer is obvious to all
Group estimates converge because members are paid to agree
e: Because the light does not actually move, there is no correct answer, so people used each other as information.
Continuing to use the group norm when alone shows it was internalized, an example of informational social influence.

q: In Asch's line-judgment experiments, many participants:
o: Gave obviously wrong answers to match the group
Changed their private beliefs about the line lengths
Conformed less when the group was unanimous
Obeyed the experimenter's orders to give wrong answers
e: This shows normative conformity: going along to fit in.

q: Labeling theory proposes that:
o: Being labeled deviant can lead people to adopt a deviant identity
Deviance arises when people lack legitimate means to reach goals
Deviance is learned through interaction with deviant peers
Weak social bonds make people more likely to act deviantly
e: Secondary deviance follows from the label.

q: A medical resident enjoys hard thinking and carefully weighs evidence. According to the elaboration likelihood model, a persuasive pamphlet will most likely influence her through:
o: The central route, based on argument quality
The peripheral route, based on attractive models
The peripheral route, based on the number of claims
Neither route, since she will resist all persuasion
e: People high in need for cognition are motivated to process messages deeply.
Deep processing means strong arguments persuade and weak ones fail, which is the central route.

q: Wearing pajamas to a formal wedding would violate a casual, everyday social norm that carries little moral weight. Such norms are called:
e: Folkways are norms for routine, casual behavior; breaking them brings mild disapproval.
Mores carry moral significance, taboos are the strongest prohibitions, and laws are formally written and enforced.

q: An attitude has which three components (the ABC model)?
e: Feelings, actions and thoughts about something.

q: People read a persuasive article that was attributed to a source with low credibility. At first they were unconvinced, but weeks later their attitudes had shifted toward the article's position. This is called:
e: Over time, people tend to remember the message but forget or detach it from its untrustworthy source.
The source's 'discount' fades, so the message gains persuasive power.

q: A hospital wants staff to wash hands more often. Posters saying 'Most of your coworkers wash their hands every time' work better than posters about germs. Which principle explains this?
o: Descriptive social norms: people follow what most others do
Injunctive norms: people follow what authorities approve of
Cognitive dissonance: people change attitudes to match actions
Obedience: people follow direct orders from authority figures
e: Highlighting what peers do creates normative influence.

q: Milgram's original obedience studies went up to 450 volts. For ethical reasons, Jerry Burger's 2009 partial replication stopped at 150 volts. Why was 150 V a reasonable stopping point for estimating obedience?
o: In Milgram's data, most who passed 150 V went on to the maximum
In Milgram's data, no participant ever obeyed past 150 V
At 150 V the learner fell silent and stopped responding
Shocks above 150 V would have injured the learner
e: At 150 V the learner first demands to be released, a key decision point.

Most of Milgram's participants who continued past it went all the way to 450 V, so 150 V predicts full obedience. Burger found about 70% continued past 150 V, not significantly different from the roughly 82% in Milgram's comparable condition.

q: A health class shows teens weak versions of tobacco ad arguments and then helps them refute each one. Later, the teens resist real tobacco ads better than classmates who did not get this training. This is:
e: McGuire's inoculation theory says exposure to weakened attacks, plus practice countering them, builds resistance to later persuasion.
It works like a vaccine, preparing 'defenses' before the real attack.

q: White participants did worse on a golf task when it was described as measuring 'natural athletic ability', while Black participants did worse when it was described as measuring 'sports intelligence'. What does this show about stereotype threat?
o: Any group can be affected when a relevant stereotype is made salient
It only affects groups that have low social status in society
Black athletes truly have less sports intelligence than white athletes
Telling people a task's purpose always lowers their scores
e: Each group underperformed only when the framing matched a negative stereotype about their own group (Stone and colleagues).
So the effect depends on the situation, not on a fixed group trait.

q: A clinic finds that patients from a minority group are less likely to be offered pain medication, even when reported pain levels are the same. Which concept best explains this pattern?
o: Bias (often implicit) leading to discrimination in care
Stereotype threat lowering patients' reports of pain
The self-serving bias among the treating clinicians
Patients' own preferences to avoid pain medication
e: Studies have documented such disparities; awareness and standardized protocols can reduce them.

q: After hearing that a stranger was robbed while walking home at night, several people say, "She should have known better." Which belief most likely drives this reaction?
e: Believing the world is fair leads people to assume victims must have done something to deserve harm.
Blaming the victim protects the feeling that 'it couldn't happen to me'.

q: A runner who exercises every day believes that very few people her age exercise regularly, though most actually do. This is the:
e: For desirable traits and abilities, people tend to underestimate how common they are, seeing themselves as unusually good.
False consensus is the opposite error, usually about opinions and undesirable behaviors.

q: Staff at one hospital describe their own team as full of different personalities, but say the staff at a rival hospital are "all the same." This illustrates:
e: People see members of their own group as varied but see out-group members as alike.
This bias makes stereotyping of out-groups easier.
t: Out-group homogeneity: 'they're all alike; we're all different.'

q: A doctor assumes a patient missed an appointment because he is irresponsible, without considering that his bus broke down. This is:
e: The fundamental attribution error: overestimating personal (dispositional) causes of OTHER people's behavior.
...while underestimating situational causes (like the bus).
Self-serving bias is about explaining your OWN successes and failures.
t: When judging others, ask: 'What situation could explain this?'
w: Self-serving bias is about your own outcomes.
The halo effect spreads one good trait to others.

q: A job applicant is polite and agreeable throughout an interview. According to correspondent inference theory (Jones and Davis), this tells observers little about her true personality mainly because:
o: Politeness is expected of anyone in that situation
Politeness is always caused by a stable inner trait
Interviews produce behavior with high distinctiveness
Observers can never make inferences about others
e: We infer dispositions most confidently from behavior that is freely chosen and unexpected (low in social desirability).
Behavior that the role demands could come from almost anyone, so it says little about the person.

q: According to the contact hypothesis, prejudice is reduced when groups:
o: Interact as equals working toward shared goals
Compete with each other for limited resources
Are kept apart to reduce chances for conflict
Learn facts about each other without direct contact
e: The jigsaw classroom technique applies this idea.

q: Participants were falsely told they were very good at telling real suicide notes from fake ones. Even after learning the feedback was made up, they still believed they had above-average skill. This is:
e: Belief perseverance is holding onto a belief after its basis has been discredited.
People build explanations for a belief, and those explanations outlast the original evidence.

q: In a 'jigsaw' classroom, each student in a mixed-ethnicity group learns one part of a lesson and must teach it to the others, because everyone is tested on the whole lesson. Prejudice drops over time. The method works mainly through:
o: Cooperative interdependence toward a shared goal
Exposure alone, without any need to cooperate
Rewards for the single best student in each group
Teacher praise for the least prejudiced students
e: Elliot Aronson's jigsaw classroom applies the contact hypothesis: equal status plus a common goal.
Each student needs every other student's piece to succeed.

q: The actor–observer bias means people tend to:
o: Explain their own behavior by situation, but others' by personality
Explain their own behavior by personality, but others' by situation
Credit successes to themselves and failures to the situation
Overestimate personality causes for everyone's behavior equally
e: Example: 'I was late because of traffic; they were late because they're lazy.'

q: The Implicit Association Test measures:
o: How quickly people pair concepts, to detect automatic associations
How strongly people endorse prejudiced statements on a survey
Physiological arousal when people view members of other groups
How accurately people recall the faces of other groups
e: Its ability to predict individual behavior is debated.

q: A bird eats berries from bushes; each bush yields berries more slowly as the bird strips it. Optimal foraging theory (the marginal value theorem) predicts that if bushes are spaced farther apart, the bird should:
o: Stay longer at each bush before moving on
Leave each bush sooner to look for richer ones
Spend the same time at each bush as before
Visit only the bushes with the most berries
e: Longer travel between patches makes leaving more costly.
So the forager should keep exploiting the current patch longer, accepting a lower intake rate before it leaves (Charnov's marginal value theorem).

q: Participants watched a woman receive painful shocks and could offer to take her place. Some were told they could easily leave if they refused. High-empathy participants offered to take her place even when leaving was easy; low-empathy participants mostly left. These results best support:
o: Social exchange theory, since helpers wanted rewards
The bystander effect, since others were watching
Kin selection, since helpers shared genes with her
e: Batson's empathy–altruism hypothesis says empathy produces truly other-focused helping.
If helping were mainly to relieve one's own distress, easy escape should have reduced it, but high-empathy people still helped.

q: Attachment styles in infants were studied using the:
e: Ainsworth identified secure, avoidant and ambivalent styles (plus later, disorganized).

q: A status is:
o: A recognized social position a person holds
The set of behaviors expected of a social position
A person's evaluation of their own social worth
A group of people who share a common identity
e: Roles are the expected behaviors attached to statuses.

q: In the Strange Situation, an infant shows little distress when her mother leaves and turns away from her when she returns. This infant is best classified as:
e: Avoidant infants show little distress at separation and ignore or avoid the caregiver at reunion.
Ambivalent infants are very distressed and are hard to comfort, often seeking and resisting contact at once.
t: Avoidant = 'I don't need you'; ambivalent = 'Don't leave, but I'm still mad.'

q: Which is an example of an achieved status?
o: Being born into a wealthy family
e: Achieved status is earned through effort or choices.
Becoming a nurse requires education and licensure.
Age, family relationships and family wealth at birth are ascribed statuses (assigned, not earned).
t: Achieved = earned. Ascribed = assigned.

q: A new graduate finds her first nursing job through a former classmate's cousin whom she met once, rather than through her close friends. This is best explained by:
o: The strength of weak ties, which reach new information
Loyalty within her primary group of close friends
The mere-exposure effect from repeated contact
Role strain within her closest friendships
e: Mark Granovetter found that acquaintances (weak ties) often link people to new networks and job leads.
Close friends tend to know the same people and information that you already know.
t: Strong ties give support; weak ties give new information.

q: A doctor acts calm and professional with patients but shares frustrations with colleagues in the break room. In Goffman's terms, the break room is the:
e: Back stage: where people relax their performance.

q: According to research on attraction, which factor most often predicts friendships and relationships?
e: People near us become familiar, increasing liking.

q: A hospital clerk refuses to admit a bleeding patient until every insurance form is filled out, even though the forms exist to support patient care. Robert Merton would call this focus on rules over goals:
e: Bureaucratic ritualism: following rules so strictly that they block the purpose they were made for.
The iron law of oligarchy (Michels) is about power concentrating in a few leaders; inertia is an organization persisting after its purpose ends.

q: In a study, roommates who were randomly assigned became friends more often than people living farther apart. Which factor does this best illustrate?
e: Random assignment rules out choosing friends based on similarity.

q: A reference group is a group that:
o: Is made up of strangers only
e: You might compare yourself with a group you hope to join.

q: Material culture includes:
o: Physical objects, like tools and buildings
Shared beliefs, like values and religion
Rules for behavior, like norms and laws
e: Non-material culture includes ideas, beliefs, values and language.

q: Mores are:
o: Shared ideas about what is desirable
e: Breaking mores (like taboos) leads to strong disapproval; folkways are casual customs.

q: The statement "If people define situations as real, they are real in their consequences" (the Thomas theorem) is most closely tied to which perspective?
e: W. I. and Dorothy Thomas stressed that people act on their interpretations of situations.
Focusing on how shared meanings guide action is the core of symbolic interactionism.

q: Country Z has 20 million people, a crude birth rate of 10 per 1,000, a crude death rate of 12 per 1,000 and net immigration of 5 per 1,000 per year. About how will its population change next year?
e: Natural increase = 10 − 12 = −2 per 1,000; adding net migration (+5) gives +3 per 1,000.
Without immigration, the country would shrink by 40,000; this is common in aging, low-fertility countries.
t: −40,000 forgets migration; +100,000 counts only migration.

q: Many jobs that once required only a high school diploma now require a college degree, although the work itself hasn't changed. Conflict theorists such as Randall Collins interpret this mainly as:
o: Credentialism that protects the advantages of privileged groups
A functional response to jobs becoming more technical
Proof that schools teach a hidden curriculum of obedience
Cultural lag between the economy and higher education
e: Collins argued that rising degree requirements act as gatekeeping, not as proof of needed skills.
Since degrees are easier for wealthier families to obtain, credentialism reproduces inequality.

q: A country has high birth rates, rapidly falling death rates and a population pyramid with a wide base. Which stage of the demographic transition is it most likely in?
e: Stage 2: death rates fall while birth rates stay high, so the population grows quickly.
w: Both rates are high in stage 1.

q: A high-fertility country's total fertility rate drops to replacement level (about 2.1), yet its population keeps growing for several more decades. The best explanation is that:
o: Large young cohorts are still entering their childbearing years
Death rates always rise once fertility rates fall
Immigration always increases when fertility drops
Replacement level actually requires 3 or more children per woman
e: Past high fertility left a young age structure with many future parents.
Even at about 2 children each, those big cohorts produce many births, so growth continues: population momentum.

q: A hospital's stated purpose is to treat patients, but it also becomes a place where neighborhood residents form friendships. The friendships are a:
e: Manifest functions are intended and recognized.
Latent functions are unintended consequences.
Friendship-building is an unintended benefit, so it's a latent function.
t: Manifest = meant. Latent = 'later noticed'.
w: It's a benefit, not a dysfunction.
A norm is an expected behavior.

q: Restlessness in children and heavy drinking were once seen as normal variation or moral failings, but are now often defined and treated as medical conditions. This process is called:
e: Medicalization is the redefining of behaviors or life experiences as medical problems.
It brings doctors' authority, diagnoses and treatments to areas once handled by family, religion or law.

q: In one year, a city of 1,000,000 people has 20,000 births, 8,000 deaths, 5,000 immigrants and 2,000 emigrants. What is its population growth rate?
e: Natural increase = 20,000 − 8,000 = 12,000; net migration = 5,000 − 2,000 = 3,000.
t: Growth = (births − deaths) + (immigrants − emigrants).

q: A country of 50 million people records 600,000 births in one year. What is its crude birth rate?
e: Crude birth rate = births ÷ population × 1,000.

q: Functionalism views society as:
o: A system of parts that work together to maintain stability
A struggle between groups over power and resources
A product of meanings created in everyday interactions
The result of individuals weighing costs and benefits
e: Associated with Durkheim and Parsons.

q: Health insurance status is an example of which kind of factor in health outcomes?
e: Social determinants include income, education, housing and access to care.

q: Melvin Tumin criticized the Davis–Moore thesis that inequality rewards the most important jobs. Which point best captures his critique?
o: Rewards often reflect power and inheritance, not importance
Inequality is truly necessary to fill society's most vital positions
Every job is paid exactly according to the skill it needs
Societies without inequality cannot fill any jobs at all
e: Tumin noted that a job's 'importance' is hard to measure and that pay often reflects bargaining power.
Stratification also blocks talented poor people from training, wasting talent instead of finding it.

q: A staff nurse leaves one hospital for a similar staff-nurse job with similar pay at another hospital. This is:
e: Horizontal mobility is moving between positions at about the same social level.
Vertical mobility involves a rise or fall in class, income or prestige.

q: In a study, Black and white patients with the same insurance and the same chest-pain symptoms were referred for cardiac catheterization at different rates. This is best described as a:
o: Healthcare disparity (a difference in care received)
Difference in disease prevalence between groups
Social gradient in health across income levels
Healthy immigrant effect among new arrivals
e: A healthcare disparity is a difference in access to or quality of care between groups.
A health disparity is a difference in health outcomes, such as disease rates or life expectancy.

q: Researchers combine blood pressure, waist size, cortisol and inflammation markers into one score of the body's cumulative wear and tear from chronic stress. This score measures:
e: Allostatic load (Bruce McEwen) is the physiological cost of repeated stress responses.
It is often higher in low-SES groups and helps explain how disadvantage gets 'under the skin'.

q: The Davis–Moore thesis, a functionalist view of stratification, argues that inequality exists because:
o: Higher rewards draw talented people into vital, demanding roles
Ruling classes use their wealth to keep workers powerless
Inequality is passed down through families' cultural capital
People are randomly assigned to social classes at birth
e: Kingsley Davis and Wilbert Moore argued that some positions matter more and need scarce talent and long training.
Unequal pay and prestige motivate people to fill them; critics note many rewards reflect power, not importance.

q: A white patient never has to wonder whether clinic staff will treat him differently because of his race. Sociologists describe this kind of unearned advantage as:
e: Privilege is an unearned advantage held by members of a dominant group, often unnoticed by them.
Cultural and social capital are resources gained from upbringing and networks.

q: In a randomized study, low-income families were offered housing vouchers to move to low-poverty neighborhoods, while a control group got no voucher. Years later, adults offered vouchers had lower rates of extreme obesity and diabetes. Why is this design especially useful?
o: Random assignment helps show neighborhoods cause health changes
It proves personal diet choices alone cause obesity
It shows that poor health causes families to move
It shows that healthier families chose better areas
e: Because vouchers were assigned at random, healthier families could not select themselves into better neighborhoods.
Differences between groups can then be attributed to the neighborhood change.

q: A woman whose parents were farmworkers earns a nursing degree and becomes a nurse manager. This is:
e: She rose above her parents' class.

q: Epidemiologists use 'incidence' to mean:
o: The number of new cases of a disease in a population during a period
The total number of existing cases in a population at one time
The number of deaths from a disease in a population during a period
The proportion of a population that is immune to a disease
e: Prevalence is the total number of existing cases at a point in time.

q: Morbidity refers to:
o: The rate of illness in a population
The rate of death in a population
The rate of births in a population
The average life expectancy in a population
e: Mortality is the death rate.

q: Country Q exports raw materials and has low wages. A modernization theorist and a dependency theorist both study why it remains poor. The dependency theorist would most likely emphasize:
o: Its history of colonial and foreign resource extraction
Its traditional values that slow economic change
Its slow adoption of new industrial technology
Its lack of a culture of savings and investment
e: Dependency theory (e.g., Andre Gunder Frank) holds that rich nations keep poor nations dependent by extracting cheap raw materials and labor.
Modernization theory (e.g., Walt Rostow) blames internal factors such as traditional values and slow technological change.

q: Hypothetical data inspired by the CDC–Kaiser Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) study are graphed: odds ratios for adult heart disease (compared with 0 ACEs) by number of childhood adversities (abuse, neglect, household dysfunction). What does the pattern most directly show?
o: A graded, dose–response link between ACEs and disease
ACEs cause heart disease in every person exposed
Only extreme adversity (4 or more) affects risk
Adult heart disease causes childhood adversity
e: Odds rise with each added ACE: 1.0 → 1.3 → 1.6 → 2.0 → 2.6.
A steady rise with exposure is a dose–response relationship; because the data are observational, they show association, not proof of cause, and odds aren't certainty.
t: Reverse causation is impossible here (childhood comes first), but confounders like family poverty remain possible.

q: The graph shows hypothetical data on household income and life expectancy. Assuming the relationship is partly causal, which conclusion is best supported?
o: A $10,000 gain adds far more years at low incomes than at high
A $10,000 gain adds the same number of years at every income level
Life expectancy stops rising once income passes $40,000
Income has no link to life expectancy above $100,000
e: From $10,000 to $20,000, life expectancy rises 3 years (72 → 75).
From $100,000 to $140,000 it rises only 1 year (83 → 84), so each extra $10,000 adds just 0.25 years.
The curve flattens, so the same income gain is linked to much larger benefits for poorer households.
t: Correlation alone can't prove income causes longer life; the stem's assumption lets you reason about policy.

q: Dexamethasone is a synthetic glucocorticoid that normally signals the brain to cut ACTH release. The graph shows hypothetical morning cortisol levels before and after a dose. What do the results for the patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) suggest?
o: Weakened negative feedback in the HPA axis
An adrenal gland that cannot make cortisol
Too little CRH released by the hypothalamus
Normal HPA regulation in both groups
e: Controls dropped from 15 to 2 µg/dL, below the 5 µg/dL cutoff: normal suppression.
Patients stayed at 10 µg/dL, so the 'stop' signal did not work well. Overactive HPA activity is a common finding in depression.

o: Any level above 50%, since effects are similar
e: Clinical response becomes likely once occupancy passes about 65%; below that, many patients do not respond.
Above about 78%, movement (extrapyramidal) side effects rise sharply, so the window of about 65–78% gives benefit with fewer side effects.

q: The table shows hypothetical results from a dual-task study of working memory. Participants hold a list of spoken digits in mind while doing a second task. Which conclusion best fits Baddeley's working memory model?
o: Verbal and spatial tasks use partly separate storage systems
All tasks draw on a single short-term store of 7 items
Spatial tapping harms verbal memory more than speaking
Repeating a word improves memory by adding rehearsal
e: Repeating a word aloud uses the phonological loop, the same system that rehearses the digits, so recall drops (7.0 → 4.5).
Spatial tapping uses the visuospatial sketchpad, so it barely affects digit recall (7.0 → 6.8).
Different amounts of interference point to separate subsystems, managed by a central executive.
